From coordinates to a tile, by hand. Which tile contains London (51.5074° N, 0.1278° W) at zoom 12? With n = 212 = 4,096: x = (lng + 180) ÷ 360 × n = (179.8722 ÷ 360) × 4,096 = 2,046.5, so x = 2,046. For y, Web Mercator uses y = (1 − ln(tan φ + sec φ) ÷ π) ÷ 2 × n; with φ = 51.5074°, tan φ = 1.2575 and sec φ = 1.6066, so ln(2.8641) = 1.0523; 1 − 1.0523 ÷ π = 0.6651; ÷ 2 × 4,096 = 1,362. The tile is 12/2046/1362, and at that latitude each pixel covers 38.2 × cos 51.5° ≈ 23.8 m. A phone screen of about 1,080 × 2,000 pixels at 256-pixel tiles shows about 5 × 8 tiles; the app adds a ring of neighbours for smooth panning, which is where "about 100 tiles per user per day" comes from.

Raster versus vector tiles. A raster tile is a picture (PNG or JPEG): simple, but every style, language, and screen density (a high-DPI phone wants 512-pixel images) needs its own copy, and zoom 18 needs its own set of 68.7 billion. A vector tile stores the geometry (road lines, building polygons, label points) and attributes in a compact binary format (the Mapbox Vector Tile spec uses protocol buffers and tile-local integer coordinates). The device draws it with the GPU. One tile set serves every style and language; rotation and tilt are free; and because geometry scales, a zoom-14 tile can be drawn at zoom 16 or 18 by overzooming — enlarging the same geometry — as long as zoom 14 stored enough detail. That single trick cuts the pyramid from 91.6 billion tiles to 358 million.

Generating and updating tiles. Tile generation is a batch job partitioned by area: for each tile, clip the source data to its bounds (plus a small buffer so lines crossing the edge join seamlessly), simplify geometry to the zoom's pixel size (no point storing a coastline wiggle smaller than a pixel), drop features too small to show, encode, and write to object storage under a versioned key. When a road is edited, regenerate only the tiles that intersect the edit at each zoom — at zoom 14 that is usually one or two tiles; at zoom 0 it is the single world tile (whose content may not change at all). Many empty tiles (open ocean) are byte-identical; store one copy and point to it, or have the server return a shared "empty" response.

Serving. Tiles are the ideal CDN object: immutable under a versioned URL, small, and popular in a heavy-tailed way (city centres at low zooms are requested constantly; a forest at zoom 14 rarely). With a 95% edge hit ratio our origin handles about 5,800 requests per second; most misses are long-tail, high-zoom tiles. Egress is the real cost: 10 billion tiles a day at 20 KB is 200 TB per day. Cutting the average tile size by 20% through better simplification saves 40 TB per day — tile size is a cost metric someone owns.

8 · Deep dive C: routing and ETA

The graph. Model the road network as a directed graph: nodes are junctions (and dead ends), edges are road segments between them, one per direction of travel (a one-way street has one edge). Each edge has a weight — the cost to traverse it. For "fastest route" the weight is travel time: length ÷ expected speed. A 600 m street at 30 km/h is 600 ÷ 8.33 m/s = 72 seconds. Turn restrictions (no left turn) and turn costs are modelled by expanding junctions into small subgraphs or by putting costs on edge pairs; we ignore them here and return to them in the deep section.

Dijkstra's algorithm. Keep a tentative distance for each node, starting at 0 for the source and infinity elsewhere, and a priority queue ordered by tentative distance. Repeatedly pop the node with the smallest distance — it is now settled, its distance final — and relax each outgoing edge: if distance(u) + weight(u, v) is less than v's tentative distance, lower it and push v. Stop when the target is settled. Trace on a tiny graph: S→A 4 min, S→B 2, B→A 1, A→T 3, B→T 7. Pop S (0): A = 4, B = 2. Pop B (2): A = min(4, 2 + 1) = 3, T = 9. Pop A (3): T = min(9, 3 + 3) = 6. Pop T (6): done, path S→B→A→T, 6 minutes. Correctness comes from non-negative weights: when a node is popped, no unexplored path can be shorter, because every such path would already cost at least as much as the popped distance.

Why it is too slow at scale. Dijkstra settles nodes in rings of increasing distance from the source. For a 300 km trip it settles every node within 300 km of travel time — in Europe, millions of nodes — and spends most of its time in villages behind the source and in the opposite direction. On a continent-sized graph that is on the order of seconds per query with a binary heap.

A* search. A* changes only the priority: instead of ordering by distance-so-far g(v), order by g(v) + h(v), where h(v) is an estimate of the remaining cost from v to the target. If h never overestimates (it is admissible), A* still returns the shortest path, and it explores far fewer nodes in the wrong direction. For travel time, the natural admissible h is straight-line distance to the target divided by the highest speed anywhere in the graph (say 130 km/h). The weakness: in a city, where actual speeds are 25 km/h, that h underestimates by a factor of five, so the search is only weakly guided. Better admissible bounds exist (landmarks: precompute distances to a few dozen landmark nodes and use the triangle inequality), but the large speed-ups come from preprocessing.

Bidirectional search. Run Dijkstra forward from the source and backward from the target (on reversed edges), alternating, and stop once the smallest tentative distances in the two queues sum to at least the best meeting path found. Two balls of radius d/2 contain roughly half the nodes of one ball of radius d on a road network, so it is about a 2× win alone — but it is the frame that contraction hierarchies build on.

Contraction hierarchies. The insight is the taxi dispatcher's: long routes go through a small set of important roads. CH makes that exact. Preprocessing: give every node an importance order. Then contract nodes from least to most important. To contract node v, remove it; for each pair of neighbours u (with an edge into v) and w (with an edge out of v) that remain, check whether the path u→v→w is the only shortest path from u to w. If it is, add a shortcut edge u→w whose weight is weight(u, v) + weight(v, w), remembering v as its middle node. If some other path from u to w avoiding v is no longer (a witness), no shortcut is needed. The check is a small local Dijkstra from u, limited in hops — the witness search.

A worked contraction: node B is a minor junction with a road from A (4 min) and a road to C (3 min). There is also a back road A→X→C costing 9 min. Contract B: the path A→B→C costs 7; the witness search from A to C without B finds only 9 > 7, so add shortcut A→C = 7 (via B). If the back road had cost 6, it would be a witness and no shortcut would be added. The paper's ordering heuristic is driven by the edge difference: shortcuts added minus edges removed when contracting v. Contracting a dead-end street removes edges and adds none, so it goes early; contracting a motorway junction would add many shortcuts, so it goes late. Remarkably, for road networks with travel-time weights the graph stays sparse throughout.

Querying: split the contracted graph's edges into "upward" edges (to a more important node) and "downward" edges. Run a bidirectional Dijkstra where the forward search from the source uses only upward edges and the backward search from the target uses only upward edges of the reversed graph. The paper proves the two searches meet at the most important node on the shortest path: any shortest path, viewed through its shortcuts, first climbs and then descends in importance. Each search climbs a short cone of local streets onto arterials and motorways, then stops. The result is a path that contains shortcuts; to produce turn-by-turn directions, recursively replace each shortcut by its two halves (via the stored middle node) until only original edges remain.

The numbers from the paper. On the Western Europe graph (18,029,721 nodes, 42,199,587 directed edges), the "economical" variant needed about 545 s of node ordering plus 57 s of hierarchy construction, and answered random queries in 223 µs settling 459 nodes; the "aggressive" variant spent about 1,627 s ordering and 170 s constructing to get 159 µs and 368 settled nodes. The extra space was negative or near zero — the search structure needs less memory than the input graph, because each edge is stored only at its less important end. Unpacking a full path took about 0.3 ms. Compared with Dijkstra's millions of settled nodes, that is the factor of thousands the estimates promised.

Live traffic and ETA. Traffic starts as probe data: anonymised location reports from phones in navigation. A GPS fix is typically accurate to several metres in the open and much worse between tall buildings, so the first step is map matching: given a sequence of noisy points, find the sequence of road segments the vehicle most likely travelled (a hidden Markov model is the classic method — candidate segments near each point are the hidden states, and transitions favour routes whose road distance matches the straight-line distance between fixes). From matched traces, each segment gets observed traversal times. A stream job (sc18) aggregates per segment over one-minute windows, discards outliers (a delivery van stopping, a bus at a bus stop), and requires several distinct vehicles before publishing a live speed. Segments without enough recent data fall back to their historical profile: the typical speed for that hour of the week, built from months of data.

The ETA is the sum over route segments of the predicted time to traverse each one at the time you reach it. A worked example for a 4-segment trip starting at 17:30:

SegmentLengthReached atSpeed usedTime
1 · local street2 km+0 minlive 40 km/h3.0 min
2 · motorway10 km+3 minlive 100 km/h6.0 min
3 · ring road (jammed now)5 km+9 minblend: live 30, profile 60 → 40 km/h7.5 min
4 · city centre1.5 km+16.5 minprofile for 17:45, 25 km/h3.6 min
Total20.1 min

Segment 3 is the interesting one. Right now it is jammed at 30 km/h, but we will reach it in 9 minutes, and jams evolve. The blend weights live data heavily for segments reached soon and shifts toward the profile for segments reached later; at 9 minutes out, a weight of 2/3 on the live 30 km/h and 1/3 on the profile's 60 km/h gives 2/3 × 30 + 1/3 × 60 = 40 km/h. Using pure live speed would say 10 minutes for that segment; pure history would say 5. Getting this blend right is where machine learning earns its place: Google's production ETA model is a graph neural network over "supersegments" — groups of adjacent road segments that share significant traffic volume — trained on past trips to predict travel time from live and historical features. Google reported it reduced negative ETA outcomes by over 40% in cities like Sydney and improved real-time ETA accuracy by up to 50% in several cities compared with the previous production system.

Combining traffic with CH. CH preprocessing assumed fixed weights, and traffic changes weights every minute. The paper's key observation is that node ordering barely depends on weights — motorways are important for a sports car and a truck alike — so you keep the order and rerun only the hierarchy construction with new weights, which took 57-88 s for Western Europe in its experiments. Newer techniques separate structure even more cleanly: multi-level overlay methods (customisable route planning, and OSRM's multi-level Dijkstra) partition the graph into cells and recompute only the boundary-to-boundary distances inside cells whose weights changed, in seconds. OSRM recommends its multi-level pipeline by default for exactly this reason, keeping CH for cases like very large distance matrices. A pragmatic alternative: compute the route with periodically refreshed weights, then evaluate the ETA along it with the freshest per-segment speeds, and re-route during the trip if a materially faster path appears.

9 · Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs

Hot cells. Cell-based partitioning puts a whole neighbourhood on one shard; a stadium or a festival makes that shard hot. Replicate the index rather than shard it (it fits in RAM), cache popular cell queries for tens of seconds, and pre-scale for known events.

Freshness versus cost. Places: a business that closed still appears until the next index patch — tolerable for minutes, not months. Tiles: a new road appears only after regeneration; a versioned rollout takes hours. Traffic: a crash shows up after map matching and aggregation, typically a minute or two; until then, routes send people into it. Each has its own freshness target, and the interview answer is to name them separately.

Cross-region routes. If each region has its own graph, a route from Paris to Berlin crosses partitions. Precompute an overlay of boundary nodes so long routes stitch through it, or keep whole continents on one machine, which the memory estimates allow.

Bad data. A missing one-way flag sends drivers the wrong way; a wrongly tagged closed road creates detours. Map data errors are the most common user-visible routing bugs, and the fix is process (validation rules, edit review, probe-based anomaly detection: if nobody ever drives a segment the graph says is open, flag it).

Graceful degradation. If the traffic pipeline fails, route on historical profiles and say ETAs may be less accurate; if the route service is overloaded, shed alternative-route computation first. If the places database is slow, serve from the index's denormalised fields without details.

Trade-offs to state at the close. Fixed cells (simple, storable in any ordered key-value store) versus quadtrees (adaptive, custom memory structure) versus S2 (adaptive covering with integer ids). Raster tiles (simple clients) versus vector tiles (one data set, client rendering, overzoom). CH (fastest queries, slower to absorb new weights) versus multi-level overlays (slightly slower queries, fast customisation). Live speeds (reactive, noisy) versus profiles (stable, blind to incidents), blended by time-to-reach.
deep:
k-nearest neighbours on a quadtree

"The 10 nearest cafés" has no radius, and guessing one is fragile: too small returns fewer than 10, too large reads too much. The exact method is a best-first search. Put the root in a priority queue keyed by its minimum distance to the query point. Repeatedly pop the closest entry: if it is a node, push its children (or, for a leaf, its points) with their distances; if it is a point, emit it. Stop after emitting k points. Because a node's key is a lower bound on any point inside it, a point is only emitted when nothing unexplored could be closer, so the result is exact and the search touches only the nodes near the answer.

Why S2 uses a Hilbert curve

Any 2-D-to-1-D mapping must break some neighbourhoods: points close on the map sometimes get far-apart ids. Geohash's Z-order curve jumps between distant parts of the square at every power-of-two boundary, so a small search region can map to many separate id ranges. The Hilbert curve is continuous — consecutive ids are always adjacent cells — so a compact region maps to fewer, longer ranges, which means fewer index seeks. Projecting onto a cube first keeps cells roughly equal in area (S2 level-13 cells range from 0.76 to 1.59 km²), whereas latitude/longitude rectangles shrink toward the poles.

Points versus shapes: when you need an R-tree

Quadtrees and cell indexes are natural for points. Roads, parks, and delivery zones are lines and polygons, and the question becomes "which shapes intersect this box" or "which zone contains this point". An R-tree groups shapes by their bounding boxes into a balanced tree of nested rectangles that may overlap; PostGIS indexes geometries this way (via GiST). Cell schemes can index shapes too, by covering each shape with a set of cells and storing it under every cell it touches, which is what S2-based systems do. The choice is about query type: point-in-polygon lookups at very high QPS (which delivery zone is this order in?) favour precomputed cell coverings.

Turn costs and restrictions

A route that makes an illegal left turn is wrong however fast it is. The clean model is an edge-based graph: make each road segment a node and each allowed turn an edge, with the turn's cost (a left turn across traffic might add 20 seconds) as its weight. This roughly triples the graph size, which is why production systems often keep the node-based graph and handle turns specially at junctions. Turn costs also break a naive CH, because the cost of passing through a junction depends on where you came from — contraction must operate on the edge-based model or carry turn tables.

Time-dependent routing

Weights that depend on the time you reach the edge (rush hour starts while you drive) make routing harder: a path that is shortest now may not be shortest when its later edges are evaluated at their arrival times. As long as the network is FIFO (first-in, first-out: leaving later never makes you arrive earlier), a time-dependent Dijkstra that evaluates each edge at its reach time stays correct. Preprocessing with time-dependent shortcuts is possible but storing a travel-time function per shortcut is expensive, so many systems use static preprocessing for the route and time-dependent evaluation for the ETA.

Alternative routes

Users want two or three sensible choices, not the shortest path plus near-copies of it. A common approach (the "via-node" method) considers paths s→v→t through candidate nodes v found in both CH search spaces, and accepts one only if it shares little with the best path (say under 80% overlap), is not much longer (say within 25%), and has no silly local detours. The CH search spaces from the main query provide the candidates almost for free.

Map matching is a decoding problem

With GPS error of tens of metres downtown, a point can lie closer to a parallel street than to the one actually driven. The hidden Markov model approach scores each candidate segment by its distance from the fix (emission probability) and each transition by how well the road distance between consecutive candidates matches the straight-line distance between fixes (transition probability), then picks the most likely sequence with the Viterbi algorithm. It is the same dynamic-programming idea used in speech recognition, and it is what turns noisy dots into segment speeds.

Location privacy is a design requirement

Probe data reveals where people live and work. Strip user identifiers at ingestion, rotate session ids frequently, drop the first and last few hundred metres of each trip (which point to home), aggregate before storing, and publish a segment speed only when several distinct vehicles contributed. These are not legal niceties: a speed computed from one car is also that car's location.
prod:
The real case: contraction hierarchies and Google's ETA model

The 2008 paper by Geisberger, Sanders, Schultes and Delling at Karlsruhe is short and readable, and its abstract states the whole idea: order nodes by importance, contract the least important node by replacing shortest paths through it with shortcuts, then answer queries with a bidirectional search where the forward search uses only edges to more important nodes and the backward search only edges from more important nodes. On a Western Europe network from the company PTV with 18,029,721 nodes and 42,199,587 directed edges (travel times derived from 13 road categories), its tuned variants answered random queries in 159-223 µs, five times faster than the best previous hierarchical technique, with negative space overhead. It also measured what matters for traffic: with the node order fixed, rebuilding the hierarchy for a different speed profile took 57-88 s. That experiment is the seed of the "structure versus weights" split every production router now uses.

Open-source routers show the lineage in practice. OSRM (the Open Source Routing Machine) implements both contraction hierarchies and multi-level Dijkstra, and its documentation recommends the multi-level pipeline by default — because it can absorb new weights quickly — while keeping CH for very large distance matrices, where CH's small search spaces win.

On the ETA side, Google's 2021 paper "ETA Prediction with Graph Neural Networks in Google Maps" describes a graph neural network deployed in production, operating on supersegments of adjacent road segments with shared traffic. The team describes what it took to make training stable, including MetaGradients to adapt the learning rate, and reports negative ETA outcomes reduced by over 40% in cities like Sydney compared with the previous production baseline. The accompanying DeepMind post adds that predictive ETAs were already accurate for over 97% of trips, and that the model improved real-time ETA accuracy by up to 50% in places like Berlin, Jakarta, São Paulo, Sydney, Tokyo and Washington D.C. The lesson for an interview: the routing algorithm and the ETA model are separate components, and the ETA is an ML system with its own data pipeline and evaluation.

Failure modes you will see

Ghost jams and phantom free-flow. A handful of probes on a quiet road, one of them a stopped delivery van, produce a fake jam; a real jam on a road with no probes stays invisible. Minimum-vehicle thresholds, outlier rejection and fallbacks to profiles are the defences; the symptom is a cluster of complaints about strange detours.

Rerouting herds. When everyone is told about the same jam, everyone takes the same side street, which then jams. Systems mitigate by spreading alternatives across users and by predicting the effect of their own advice — a feedback loop with no parallel in ordinary web services.

Stale tiles after edits. If tiles are cached under unversioned URLs with long TTLs, a corrected road keeps its old drawing for days. Versioned URLs make the rollout explicit and instant once clients switch.

Index rebuild failures. A nightly quadtree or cell-index rebuild that fails leaves yesterday's data in place — fine — but one that "succeeds" with a corrupt input (say, coordinates swapped latitude for longitude) puts every café in the ocean. Validate rebuilt indexes against a sample of known queries before swapping them in.

What to monitor

Search: p50/p99 latency, candidates scanned per query (a jump means cells are too large or an index regression), zero-result rate. Tiles: edge hit ratio, origin request rate, average tile bytes, egress per day. Routing: query latency and settled-node counts, customisation lag (age of weights in use), share of segments running on live versus profile speeds. ETA: error distribution on completed trips, especially the rate of large underestimates, broken down by city and time of day. Traffic pipeline: probe ingest rate, map-matching failure rate, end-to-end lag from probe to published speed.
myths: The nearest places are the ones in my geohash cell.

Cells are rectangles with arbitrary edges. A café 30 m away across a boundary can have a completely different geohash, and a cell may be empty while its neighbour is full. A correct search covers the search circle with the cell and its neighbours (or with a set of S2 cells), then filters candidates by true distance.
A longer geohash is always better because it is more precise.

Precision is a trade-off. Cells smaller than the search radius force you to scan dozens or hundreds of cells per query; cells far bigger than the radius return thousands of candidates to filter. Pick the precision whose cell is about the size of the radius, and remember cells get narrower in kilometres as you move away from the equator.
Google Maps runs Dijkstra's algorithm for every route.

Plain Dijkstra on a continent-sized road graph settles millions of nodes per query. Production routers preprocess the graph — contraction hierarchies, multi-level overlays or similar — so a query settles hundreds of nodes. In the original contraction-hierarchies paper, queries on an 18-million-node Western Europe graph took about 0.16-0.22 ms.
The map you see is a set of pictures generated when you look at it.

Map imagery is pre-cut into a pyramid of tiles addressed by zoom/x/y, generated ahead of time (or on first request and cached), and served from CDNs. Modern apps download vector tiles — geometry plus attributes — and draw them on the device, so one tile set serves every style, language and screen density.
ETA is distance divided by the speed limit.

ETA is the sum of predicted travel times for every road segment at the moment you will reach it. Near segments use live speeds from phones on the road; far segments use what traffic is predicted to be when you get there, from historical patterns; a learned model corrects the sum. Speed limits are only a fallback when no data exists.
Live traffic needs a perfectly fresh global graph.

Traffic changes edge weights, not the road network's structure. Systems keep the expensive preprocessing that depends on structure and rerun only a fast 'customisation' step with new weights every few minutes, or apply live weights only near the start of the route. Freshness of tens of seconds to a few minutes is the realistic target.
lab:
Goal: build a point quadtree, run radius searches, and confirm against brute force that it returns exactly the same places while reading far fewer. Python 3.12, standard library only, a few seconds.

"""Point quadtree with split-on-overflow and radius search, checked against brute force."""
import math, random, time

class Node:
    __slots__ = ("x0", "y0", "x1", "y1", "pts", "kids")
    def __init__(self, x0, y0, x1, y1):
        self.x0, self.y0, self.x1, self.y1 = x0, y0, x1, y1
        self.pts, self.kids = [], None

CAP = 32

def insert(n, p):
    while n.kids:                                   # descend to the leaf containing p
        mx, my = (n.x0 + n.x1) / 2, (n.y0 + n.y1) / 2
        n = n.kids[(p[0] >= mx) + 2 * (p[1] >= my)]  # 0=SW 1=SE 2=NW 3=NE
    n.pts.append(p)
    if len(n.pts) > CAP and n.x1 - n.x0 > 1e-6:     # split on overflow
        mx, my = (n.x0 + n.x1) / 2, (n.y0 + n.y1) / 2
        n.kids = [Node(n.x0, n.y0, mx, my), Node(mx, n.y0, n.x1, my),
                  Node(n.x0, my, mx, n.y1), Node(mx, my, n.x1, n.y1)]
        pts, n.pts = n.pts, []
        for q in pts: insert(n, q)

def box_dist(n, x, y):                              # min distance from (x, y) to the box
    dx = max(n.x0 - x, 0, x - n.x1); dy = max(n.y0 - y, 0, y - n.y1)
    return math.hypot(dx, dy)

def radius(n, x, y, r, out, stats):
    stats["nodes"] += 1
    if box_dist(n, x, y) > r: return                # prune the whole subtree
    if n.kids:
        for k in n.kids: radius(k, x, y, r, out, stats)
    else:
        stats["points"] += len(n.pts)
        out.extend(p for p in n.pts if math.hypot(p[0] - x, p[1] - y) <= r)

random.seed(1)
W = 100.0                                           # a 100 km x 100 km region
city = [(random.gauss(30, 2), random.gauss(70, 2)) for _ in range(150_000)]   # dense centre
rural = [(random.uniform(0, W), random.uniform(0, W)) for _ in range(50_000)]
places = [(min(max(x, 0), W - 1e-9), min(max(y, 0), W - 1e-9)) for x, y in city + rural]
root = Node(0, 0, W, W)
t = time.perf_counter()
for p in places: insert(root, p)
print(f"built {len(places):,} points in {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")

for (x, y, r) in [(30, 70, 0.5), (30, 70, 2.0), (80, 20, 5.0)]:
    out, stats = [], {"nodes": 0, "points": 0}
    radius(root, x, y, r, out, stats)
    brute = [p for p in places if math.hypot(p[0] - x, p[1] - y) <= r]
    print(f"q=({x},{y}) r={r} km: {len(out)} found, brute {len(brute)}, "
          f"same={sorted(out) == sorted(brute)}, nodes visited {stats['nodes']}, "
          f"points checked {stats['points']:,} of {len(places):,}")
  1. Run it. Every query should print same=True: pruning by box distance never loses a valid answer, because a box's minimum distance is a lower bound for every point inside it.
  2. Compare "points checked" with 200,000. In the dense centre with r = 0.5 km, the tree reads a few thousand points to find a few hundred; in the rural query with r = 5 km it reads a few hundred. Brute force reads all 200,000 every time.
  3. Change CAP to 4 and to 512. Small capacity means a deeper tree (more nodes visited, fewer wasted point checks); large capacity means a shallow tree that checks many more points. The best value balances node overhead against per-point checks.
  4. Replace the quadtree with a fixed grid of 1 km cells (a dictionary keyed by (int(x), int(y))) and compare points checked for the dense query and the rural query: the grid wastes work in the city or in the countryside depending on the cell size you choose — the density problem from the lesson.
recap: A maps product is three systems: proximity search over places, a tile pipeline that draws the map, and a routing engine that answers 'how do I get there and how long will it take'.

Proximity search turns two-dimensional coordinates into cells; choose a cell size near the search radius, cover the circle with the cell and its neighbours, then filter by real (haversine) distance and rank.
A quadtree adapts cell size to density by splitting a square into four whenever it holds more than a set number of points, so Manhattan gets tiny cells and the desert stays one big cell.
Radius search on a quadtree visits only nodes whose bounding box comes within the radius of the query point; everything else is pruned without being read.

The map is a pyramid of 256-pixel tiles: zoom z has 4^z tiles, each zoom level halves the metres per pixel, and the full pyramid to zoom 18 is about 92 billion tiles, so most are never rendered and vector tiles stop at about zoom 14.
Tiles are immutable files addressed by zoom/x/y, which makes them ideal for CDNs; the hit ratio sets origin load and egress cost.

Dijkstra explores outward in rings; A* adds an admissible heuristic to aim the search; contraction hierarchies preprocess the graph with shortcuts so a query only climbs to more important nodes from both ends.
Contracting a node adds a shortcut between two neighbours only when the path through that node is the unique shortest path, which a small witness search checks.

ETA sums per-segment travel times evaluated at the time you will reach each segment, mixing live probe speeds, historical profiles and an ML correction, which Google reported improved with graph neural networks.
The hard operational problems are freshness (traffic and map edits), hotspots, cross-region routes and protecting the location data that feeds traffic.
glossary: Dijkstra's algorithm with a heuristic added to each node's priority: the estimated remaining cost to the goal. If the estimate never overestimates, A* still finds the shortest path while exploring fewer nodes.
An estimate of remaining cost that is never larger than the true remaining cost, such as straight-line distance divided by the maximum road speed.
Running one search forward from the start and one backward from the goal and stopping when they meet.
The smallest axis-aligned rectangle that contains a shape or a set of points.
A network of cache servers near users that serves repeated requests for the same files without going back to the origin.
A routing speed-up that ranks nodes by importance, removes them one by one while adding shortcut edges to preserve shortest paths, then answers queries with two small upward searches.
Recomputing shortcut weights for new edge costs (such as live traffic) without redoing the expensive structural preprocessing.
The classic shortest-path algorithm: repeatedly settle the unvisited node with the smallest known distance and relax its outgoing edges.
The cost of traversing a road segment in the routing graph, usually travel time rather than distance.
The predicted travel time (or arrival clock time) for a route.
A string naming a rectangle on Earth, made by interleaving longitude and latitude bits; each extra character makes the cell 32 times smaller in area.
The formula for the great-circle distance between two latitude/longitude points on a sphere.
Snapping a noisy sequence of GPS points to the road segments the vehicle actually travelled.
Drawing a tile at a higher zoom than it was generated for by scaling up its geometry; used so vector tiles can stop at about zoom 14.
A place users search for: a shop, restaurant, station, landmark.
Anonymised location and speed reports from phones or vehicles moving on roads, used to estimate traffic.
A tree that recursively divides a square into four equal quadrants; a point quadtree splits a node when it holds too many points.
In Dijkstra, check whether reaching a neighbour through the current node is shorter than its best known distance, and update it if so.
Google's library that projects the sphere onto a cube and subdivides each face as a quadtree, numbering cells along a Hilbert curve into 64-bit ids.
A node whose shortest distance Dijkstra has finalised.
In contraction hierarchies, an added edge whose weight equals the length of a shortest path through one or more contracted nodes.
A square piece of the map at one zoom level, addressed by zoom, x and y, typically 256 or 512 pixels across.
The set of all tiles for all zoom levels: one tile at zoom 0, four at zoom 1, and 4^z at zoom z.
A tile that stores geometry and attributes (roads, labels, buildings) rather than pixels; the device styles and draws it.
The map projection used by web maps; it keeps shapes locally correct but stretches areas near the poles, and is cut off at about 85.05° latitude to make the world square.
During contraction, a short local search for a path between two neighbours that avoids the node being contracted; if one exists that is no longer, no shortcut is needed.
drill:
Work it out

You are designing "nearby restaurants" for a city app with 2 million places in one metro area of 50 km × 50 km. Two thirds of the places are in a 5 km × 5 km downtown. Queries use a 500 m radius and return the top 20. (a) What geohash precision would you choose, and how many candidates does a downtown query read? (b) What about a suburban one? (c) What do you change?

Answer

(a) For 500 m, precision 6 (about 1.2 km × 0.6 km at the equator; narrower east-west at higher latitudes) is the longest precision whose cell is at least the radius, so search the 3×3 block: about 3.7 × 1.8 km ≈ 6.7 km². Downtown density is 2,000,000 × 2/3 ÷ 25 km² ≈ 53,000 places per km², so the block holds about 6.7 × 53,000 ≈ 355,000 candidates — to return 20. Even at 50 ns per distance check that is about 18 ms of CPU per query before ranking, and it is a lot of memory traffic.

(b) The rest of the area holds 667,000 places over 2,475 km² ≈ 270 per km², so a suburban 3×3 block holds about 1,800 candidates — fine.

(c) The fixed grid is right for the suburbs and wrong downtown by two orders of magnitude. Options: (1) use a quadtree with a capacity of about 100, so downtown leaves become tens of metres across and a 500 m search touches a few hundred leaves of up to 100 points each — the circle's area holds about 0.79 × 53,000 ≈ 42,000 places, so you read a little more than that; (2) cover the circle with S2 cells of mixed levels to cut the 8.5× area waste of the 3×3 block; (3) most importantly, question the product: 42,000 places genuinely lie within 500 m downtown, so reading them all to rank 20 is wasteful. Shrink the radius adaptively (expand from 100 m until you have, say, 500 candidates), or pre-rank each leaf's places by quality so you scan only the top few per leaf. The general lesson: in dense areas, the cost is set by how many places are genuinely inside the radius, and the fix is adaptive radius plus per-cell pre-ranking, not a cleverer index alone.

Estimate it

Your vector tiles average 25 KB, users load 120 tiles per day, and you have 50 million DAU. The CDN charges $0.02 per GB of egress and your origin charges $0.09 per GB. The edge hit ratio is 92%. What is the daily egress bill, and what is a 1-point hit-ratio improvement worth?

Answer

Tiles per day: 50M × 120 = 6 billion. Bytes: 6 × 109 × 25 KB = 150 × 1012 B = 150 TB/day = 150,000 GB. All of it leaves the CDN to users: 150,000 × $0.02 = $3,000/day. Misses (8%) also cross from origin to CDN: 12,000 GB × $0.09 = $1,080/day. Total about $4,080/day, roughly $1.5M a year.

Each hit-ratio point moves 1% of traffic, 1,500 GB/day, off the origin: 1,500 × $0.09 = $135/day, about $49,000 a year, plus 60 million fewer origin requests per day (6 billion × 1%), about 2.5 million per hour. Cutting average tile size by 20% would save 20% of both lines, about $816/day — usually the bigger lever. The point to make out loud: for a tile service, bytes per tile and hit ratio are cost metrics with owners, not just performance metrics.
qa: E
How would you find all restaurants within 1 km of a user?

Map each place to a cell key (geohash, S2 or a quadtree leaf) and index places by that key. For a query, pick a cell size near 1 km, take the user's cell plus its neighbours so the whole circle is covered, read the candidates, compute the real haversine distance, keep those within 1 km, and rank by distance, rating and relevance. The cell lookup is a cheap filter; the distance check is what makes the answer correct.

Follow-up: Why not a SQL query with lat BETWEEN and lng BETWEEN? — Two range conditions on two columns cannot both use one B+ tree efficiently: the index narrows latitude to a band around the whole planet and then scans it. A cell key turns two dimensions into one sortable key.
E
What is a map tile and why are maps served that way?

A tile is a fixed square of the map at one zoom level, addressed by zoom/x/y. Cutting the world into a fixed grid means every client asks for the same few URLs for the same view, so tiles are immutable, cache perfectly in CDNs, and load in parallel. Panning fetches only the new edge tiles.
E
Why does a proximity search look in neighbouring cells?

Because cell boundaries are arbitrary lines: a place a few metres from the user can sit across the boundary in a different cell, and a user near a corner has the circle spilling into up to three other cells. Checking the 3×3 block guarantees coverage when the cell is at least as large as the radius.
M
How do you choose a geohash precision for a 500 m search?

Choose the precision whose cell is at least about the radius in both directions: precision 6 is about 1.2 km by 0.6 km at the equator, so a 3×3 block covers any 500 m circle centred in the middle cell. Precision 7 (about 150 m) would need many more cells; precision 5 (about 4.9 km) would return roughly 70 times more candidates to filter. Away from the equator the east-west size shrinks with the cosine of latitude, so at 60° the precision-6 cell is about 0.6 km wide.

Follow-up: What if the area is extremely dense? — Fixed cells then return too many candidates; an adaptive structure such as a quadtree, or covering with smaller S2 cells, keeps candidates per cell bounded.
M
Explain how a point quadtree is built and searched.

Start with one square covering the area. Insert points into it; when a node exceeds its capacity (say 100 points), split it into four equal quadrants and move its points into the children. For a radius search, start at the root, skip any node whose bounding box is farther than the radius from the query point, recurse into the rest, and at leaves check each point's true distance. Dense areas end up with deep, small leaves and empty areas stay shallow.

Follow-up: How do you find the k nearest instead of within a radius? — Use a priority queue ordered by each node's minimum possible distance; pop nodes and points in that order and stop once you have k points closer than the next node's minimum distance.
M
How many tiles are there at zoom 18 and how would you store them?

Zoom z has 4^z tiles, so zoom 18 has about 68.7 billion and the whole pyramid to 18 about 92 billion. Most of them are ocean or empty land, so you never pre-render them all: pre-generate low zooms, render high zooms on first request and cache, deduplicate identical empty tiles, and with vector tiles stop generating at about zoom 14 (about 358 million tiles in total) and let the client overzoom.

Follow-up: How do map edits reach users? — Re-render only the tiles that touch the edited geometry at each zoom, publish them under a new version, and let clients fetch the new version; never rely on purging old tiles from every CDN.
M
Compare Dijkstra, A* and bidirectional search for routing.

Dijkstra expands nodes in order of distance from the start, in rings, so it explores everything closer than the destination. A* adds a heuristic estimate of remaining distance to aim the search toward the goal; with an admissible heuristic it is still exact. Bidirectional search runs from both ends and meets in the middle, exploring roughly two half-size balls instead of one full one. On road graphs all three remain far too slow for continental queries at scale, which is why preprocessing exists.

Follow-up: Why is the A* heuristic weak for travel time? — Straight-line distance divided by the highest motorway speed badly underestimates urban travel times, so the guide is loose and A* explores much of what Dijkstra would.
M
How are live traffic speeds produced?

Phones in navigation send anonymised location samples. Map matching snaps each trace to road segments; the time to traverse each segment gives an observed speed. A stream job aggregates observations per segment over a short window, drops outliers, and requires a minimum number of distinct vehicles before trusting the value. Where there is too little data it falls back to the segment's historical speed for that hour of the week.
Follow-up: What breaks at night or on rural roads? — Sparse probes: one slow vehicle could look like a jam, so you require several vehicles, widen the window and weight toward history.
M
How would you compute an ETA for a 40-minute route?

Sum the predicted traversal time of each segment at the time you will reach it. Segments in the first few minutes use live speeds; later ones blend live speed toward the historical profile for the predicted arrival time, because today's jam may clear by then. A learned model then corrects the total using route-level features. Return the distribution's central value, and recompute during the trip as conditions change.

Follow-up: How do you measure ETA quality? — Compare predicted and actual arrival for completed trips: mean absolute error, the share within ±10%, and the rate of large underestimates, which users punish most.
H
Explain contraction hierarchies.

Order nodes by importance (local streets low, motorway junctions high). Contract them from least important: remove a node and, for each pair of its neighbours, add a shortcut edge if the path through it is the only shortest path, which a small witness search checks. A query then runs Dijkstra upward from the source and upward (in reverse) from the target, using only edges toward more important nodes; the searches meet at the highest node on the shortest path. In the 2008 paper this answered Western Europe queries (18 million nodes) in about 0.16-0.22 ms, settling a few hundred nodes.

Follow-up: How do you get the actual turn-by-turn route? — Shortcuts store the contracted middle node, so you recursively unpack each shortcut into its two halves until only original edges remain; the paper measured about 0.3 ms for unpacking.
H
How do you keep routing fast when traffic changes edge weights every minute?

Separate structure from weights. The node order and shortcut topology depend mostly on the road network, which changes slowly; the shortcut weights depend on traffic. Recompute only weights (customisation) every few minutes, which the CH paper showed takes about a minute for Western Europe and multi-level overlay methods do in seconds; or apply live weights only around the start of the route and use profiles beyond. This is why OSRM recommends its multi-level Dijkstra pipeline by default.

Follow-up: What about time-dependent weights? — Use per-segment speed profiles by time of day; the query evaluates each edge at the time it is reached, which makes the search harder and is often approximated by profile buckets.
H
How would you partition a world road graph across machines?

Partition by region with few cut edges (natural borders, mountains, water), so most routes are answered inside one partition. Precompute an overlay graph of boundary nodes with shortest distances between them, so long routes stitch partitions together without loading every region. Replicate each partition for read throughput, because the graph is read-only between customisations.
Follow-up: How big is the graph per machine? — A continental graph of tens of millions of nodes fits in a few gigabytes, so the motivation is throughput and blast radius as much as memory.
H
How would this change if an LLM or ML model were in the path, for example 'find a quiet café with good Wi-Fi near me, open now'?

The geo index becomes a filter and the language model handles meaning. Parse the request into structured constraints (category café, open now, radius) and a semantic part (quiet, good Wi-Fi). Use the cell index to fetch candidates within the radius, then rank them by embedding similarity between the query and review text, plus rating and distance, and let an LLM write the answer citing those places. Filter first: a global vector search followed by a distance filter returns nothing nearby or wastes the top-k on far-away matches.

Follow-up: Where else does ML sit in a maps stack? — ETA prediction (a graph neural network at Google), map matching, traffic anomaly detection and extracting places and road features from imagery; each is a model with its own freshness and evaluation loop.
H
A stadium concert ends and 50,000 phones search for nearby restaurants and request routes at once. What breaks?

The geo index shard holding that area becomes hot, because cell-based partitioning puts the whole neighbourhood on one shard; replicate hot cells or cache popular query results per cell for tens of seconds. Routing load spikes for one region; precomputed CH queries are cheap, so it is usually the traffic feed and ETA model calls that saturate. Live speeds drop sharply around the venue, which is correct but must not be smoothed away. Prepare by scaling for known events.
Follow-up: How do you cache a nearby search? — Key by cell id at a fixed precision plus filters, store the top N candidates, and compute the final distance ordering per user.

t: Design a distributed rate limiter service
sum: Shared counters for a fleet of gateways: the four algorithms replayed on one trace, the race in a naive INCR + EXPIRE and the atomic Lua fix, local versus global limits and their accuracy/latency trade-off, multi-region limits, fail-open versus fail-closed, and rate-limiting LLM tokens.
prereq: ld2
Fixed window, sliding-window log, sliding-window counter and token bucket, built inside one process: what each stores per key and how each treats bursts.
sc12
Rate limiting caps what each client may send; load shedding drops work when the server itself is overloaded; retries without backoff amplify overload.
sc2
An API gateway sits in front of services and runs per-request policy (authentication, routing, limits) before forwarding.
in3
Redis is a single-threaded in-memory store sharded by key slot; each command is atomic, and replication to replicas is asynchronous.
os4
A race condition happens when two actors read shared state and then write based on what they read, with the other's write landing in between.
sc17
Multi-region systems trade consistency for latency: cross-region round trips cost tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
why:
It is 02:13 and the on-call engineer for a payments API is paged: latency on every endpoint has tripled. The cause, found twenty minutes later, is a single customer whose nightly reconciliation script has a bug — it retries every failed call immediately, forever, from 400 threads. That one customer is now sending 30,000 requests per second, and the database behind the API is spending its time on them while every other customer times out. There is a rate limit of 100 requests per second per API key, written into the gateway years ago. It is enforced separately on each of 60 gateway machines, so the customer is actually allowed 6,000 per second. And the counters reset at the top of every second, so even that is exceeded in bursts.

A rate limiter exists so that one client, by accident or on purpose, cannot consume capacity that belongs to everyone. Inside one process it is a small algorithm — a counter or a bucket of tokens — and the low-level design case ld2 builds those. The problem changes completely when the limit must hold across a fleet: dozens or hundreds of gateway nodes in several regions, each seeing a slice of each client's traffic, all needing to agree on one count, within a millisecond, for every single request, without the limiter itself becoming the thing that takes the API down.

That is a distributed systems problem in miniature. Shared counters invite races. A central store adds a network hop and a dependency. Local counters are fast but disagree. Regions are 100 ms apart. Clocks differ. And the limiter must decide what to do when its own store is unreachable — allow everything, or reject everything — which is a business decision dressed as a technical one.

This lesson works through the design in interview order: requirements; estimates (decisions per second, store sizing, memory per algorithm, latency budget); the API and rule model; the high-level design and the critical path of one check; then three deep dives. The first replays fixed window, sliding log, sliding counter and token bucket on the same request trace, so their differences are concrete. The second is the race in a naive Redis INCR + EXPIRE and the atomic Lua fix. The third is local versus global limits, multi-region limits, and fail-open versus fail-closed. The real cases are Stripe's account of its four limiters and Cloudflare's per-data-centre counting; the lab replays all four algorithms on one trace and reproduces the check-then-act race.
primer:
The mental model: one club, many doors, one clicker

Picture a nightclub with a fire limit of 300 people. With one door and one bouncer holding a clicker, enforcing it is trivial: click in, click out, stop at 300. Now the club opens six doors to handle the queue. Each bouncer has a clicker, and each sees only the people at their door. If each stops at 50 (300 ÷ 6), the limit holds — until one door gets twice the queue of the others and turns people away while the club is half empty. If each bouncer radios the others before letting anyone in, the count is right, but every entry waits for a radio call, and if the radio dies, nobody knows what to do. The compromises are the interesting part: bouncers report their counts every minute; or the manager hands each bouncer a strip of 20 wristbands, and they come back for more when they run out.

Every piece of that maps onto the design. The doors are gateway nodes behind a load balancer. The clicker is a counter or token bucket per client key. The radio is a call to a shared store (Redis is the usual choice). Reporting every minute is periodic synchronisation; the strip of wristbands is a token lease. The question of what to do when the radio fails is fail-open versus fail-closed.

The analogy breaks in two useful places. A club has one fire limit; an API has many overlapping limits per request — per API key, per endpoint, per IP address, per organisation — all checked together. And a person is one unit, while requests differ hugely in cost: a cheap read, an expensive search, an LLM call generating 4,000 tokens. The limiter has to count in the right units.

What the service actually does

Strip away the algorithms and a rate limiter service answers one question per request: given these descriptors (who is calling, what they are calling) and this cost, allow or reject — and if rejecting, when should they retry? The answer must come back in about a millisecond, because it sits on the path of every request. It must be correct enough that a misbehaving client is actually stopped, and cheap enough that checking does not cost more than the requests it protects. And it must degrade gracefully, because a limiter that fails by rejecting everything is an outage you built yourself.

Where the limiter lives

You can put the limiting logic in three places, and an interviewer will ask why you chose one. In the client library: cheap, but you do not control clients. In the gateway or sidecar in front of services (sc2): every request passes through it, it knows the API key after authentication, and it can reject before any backend work happens — the usual answer. Or as a separate rate-limit service that gateways call over the network (Envoy's global rate limit service works this way): rules and logic are centralised, at the cost of one more network hop. A common compromise is a thin limiter client library inside the gateway that talks directly to Redis, with rules pushed from a central service — the shape drawn above.

1 · Requirements

Functional. (1) Define rules: a limit (for example 100 requests per second, or 1,000 per minute) on a combination of descriptors — API key, organisation, endpoint, IP address, user tier. (2) For each request, check all matching rules with a cost (default 1) and return allow or reject, the remaining allowance and the time until reset. (3) Return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header on rejection, and rate-limit headers on every response. (4) Change rules at runtime without deploys, including shadow mode (log what would be rejected without rejecting). (5) Expose metrics: decisions per rule and key, top limited keys. Out of scope, said aloud: billing-grade monthly quotas (which need durable exact counting — mention it as a separate system), DDoS mitigation at the network layer (net14), and bot detection.

Non-functional. Added latency under about 1 ms at p50 and 2-5 ms at p99. Accuracy: within a few percent of the configured limit; small overshoot is acceptable, systematic under-admission of good clients is not. Availability: the limiter must never be the reason the API is down. Scale: hundreds of thousands to millions of decisions per second across regions. Fairness: one client cannot consume another's allowance.

Clarifying questions. What is being protected — capacity (so approximate is fine) or money (so be strict)? Are limits per second, per minute, per day? Does the limit need to be global across regions, or per region? Do requests have different costs (an LLM call counts tokens)? What should happen if the limiter's store is down? The answers pick the algorithm and the failure policy.

2 · Back-of-envelope estimates

Assume an API platform with 500,000 requests per second at peak across 3 regions, 10 million active API keys, and 3 rules checked per request (per key per second, per key per endpoint per minute, per IP per minute).

Checks per second. 500,000 × 3 = 1.5 million rule evaluations per second. If all three rules for a request are evaluated in one call to the store (possible when their keys live on the same shard, explained below), that is 500,000 store calls per second.

Store throughput. Redis executes commands on one thread per shard; a small Lua script doing a few hash reads and writes takes on the order of tens of microseconds. Plan conservatively for 50,000 script calls per second per shard: 500,000 ÷ 50,000 = 10 primaries worldwide, 15-20 with 50% headroom, each with a replica. Per region, the busiest might carry 40% of traffic: 200,000 calls per second, 6-8 primaries.

Memory, by algorithm. A token bucket needs two numbers per key and rule (tokens, last refill time); stored as a small Redis hash with its key name and overhead, about 100 bytes. 10M keys × 3 rules × 100 B = 3 GB. A fixed window or sliding-window counter is similar (one or two counters). A sliding-window log stores one entry per accepted request in the window: at a limit of 1,000 per minute, a busy key has up to 1,000 sorted-set entries at roughly 64 bytes each — 64 KB per key. If even 1 million keys were near their limits, that is 64 GB for one rule, and 10 million would be 640 GB. That single estimate is why logs are reserved for low limits.

Latency budget. If the API's p99 target is 200 ms, the limiter can have 2-5 ms of it. An in-region round trip to Redis is roughly 0.2-1 ms, which fits. A cross-region round trip is 50-150 ms, which does not: global limits cannot be checked synchronously across regions on every request. The estimate decides a later deep dive.

Bandwidth. A check request and reply are a few hundred bytes: 500,000 × 300 B = 150 MB/s spread across gateways and shards — not a constraint.

3 · The API

Two APIs: the internal check API the gateway uses, and what the end client sees.

POST /v1/ratelimit/check                      (internal; usually gRPC)
  {domain: "public_api",
   descriptors: [{api_key: "k_123"}, {api_key: "k_123", route: "/v1/search"}, {ip: "203.0.113.7"}],
   cost: 1}
  → {decision: "OVER_LIMIT",
     statuses: [{rule: "key_per_sec",  limit: 100,  remaining: 0,  reset_after_ms: 400},
                {rule: "key_route_min", limit: 1000, remaining: 212, reset_after_ms: 31000},
                {rule: "ip_per_min",   limit: 600,  remaining: 590, reset_after_ms: 52000}]}

Client response on rejection:
  HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
  Retry-After: 1
  RateLimit-Limit: 100
  RateLimit-Remaining: 0
  RateLimit-Reset: 1
  {"error": {"type": "rate_limit_error", "message": "100 requests/second per API key exceeded"}}

A request is allowed only if every matching rule allows it, and a rejected request should not consume allowance from the rules that would have allowed it — a detail the multi-rule script in deep dive B handles by deciding every rule before spending from any. 429 is defined in RFC 6585; the RateLimit-* header names come from an IETF draft, and many APIs still use their own X-RateLimit-* names. The point is that clients can see their remaining budget and slow down before they hit the wall.

4 · The data model

rules (config store, versioned, pushed to gateways):
  {id: "key_per_sec", domain: "public_api", match: {api_key: "*"},
   algorithm: "token_bucket", capacity: 100, refill_per_sec: 100,
   shadow: false, fail_mode: "open"}
  {id: "login_per_ip", match: {route: "/login", ip: "*"},
   algorithm: "sliding_counter", limit: 10, window_s: 60, fail_mode: "closed"}

counters (Redis, sharded by hash tag, all with TTLs):
  rl:{k_123}:key_per_sec          → hash {tokens: 37.5, ts: 1767000000.123}
  rl:{k_123}:key_route_min:/v1/search:29450000 → integer (current window count)
  rl:{ip:203.0.113.7}:ip_per_min:29450000      → integer

The braces are a Redis Cluster hash tag: only the part inside {…} is hashed to pick a shard, so every counter for API key k_123 lands on the same shard and one script can read and update them together. The IP rule has a different tag and may live elsewhere, so in practice per-key rules are batched into one call and the IP rule is a second call (or is enforced locally). Every counter carries a TTL (time to live: an expiry after which Redis deletes the key) so idle keys disappear; nothing about a rate limit needs to live longer than its window.

5 · High-level design and the critical path

One request, step by step: (1) The load balancer sends it to any gateway node. (2) The gateway authenticates it and extracts descriptors (API key, route, client IP). (3) It matches descriptors against its cached rules — a pure in-memory step. (4) For the key's rules, it calls the Redis shard owning {k_123} with one Lua script, passing each rule's parameters and the cost. The script reads the counters, refills or slides them, decides for all rules, and only if all allow, spends from all of them; it returns the decision and remaining counts. (5) The gateway adds rate-limit headers and either forwards the request or returns 429. (6) It emits a decision metric asynchronously. Total added latency: one in-region round trip plus microseconds of script time.

Around this path sit the rules service (stores rule versions, validates them, pushes them to gateways, supports shadow mode and gradual rollout) and observability (which keys are being limited, by which rule, and how often the limiter failed open). The limiter client in each gateway also holds a local token bucket per key as a coarse backstop for when Redis is slow or unreachable.

6 · Deep dive A: four algorithms on one request trace

ld2 builds the four algorithms inside one process. Here the point is to see how differently they behave on the same traffic, because choosing between them is a product decision. The rule is 4 requests per 10 seconds. A single client sends 12 requests at t = 1, 6, 8, 9, 9.5, 10.5, 11, 12, 14, 17, 19 and 23 seconds. For the windows, "window 0" is [0, 10), "window 1" is [10, 20) and "window 2" is [20, 30).

Fixed window. Count accepted requests per window; reject when the window's count has reached 4. Window 0 accepts t = 1, 6, 8, 9 and rejects 9.5. At t = 10 the count resets: 10.5, 11, 12 and 14 are accepted, then 17 and 19 rejected. Window 2 accepts 23. Total accepted: 9. Look at the 8 seconds from t = 6 to t = 14: 7 requests got through against a limit of 4 per 10 s — nearly twice the limit, because the boundary at t = 10 wiped the count. That is the fixed window's defining flaw.

Sliding-window log. Keep the timestamp of each accepted request; a new request is allowed if fewer than 4 accepted timestamps fall in the trailing 10 seconds (t − 10, t]. At t = 9.5 the log holds 1, 6, 8, 9 → reject. At 10.5 the window is (0.5, 10.5], still 4 → reject. At 11 the window (1, 11] has dropped t = 1 → 3 → accept. At 12 and 14: 6, 8, 9, 11 → reject. At 17: (7, 17] holds 8, 9, 11 → accept. At 19: (9, 19] holds 11, 17 → accept (9 has just left). At 23: accept. Total 8, and no 10-second span ever holds more than 4. Exact — at the price of storing every timestamp.

Sliding-window counter. Keep only the counts for the current and previous fixed windows, and estimate the trailing-window count as previous × (fraction of the previous window still inside the trailing window) + current, assuming the previous window's requests were evenly spread. Allow if the estimate plus this request's cost is at most 4. At t = 10.5: previous = 4, 0.5 s into window 1 so 95% of the previous window overlaps: 4 × 0.95 + 0 = 3.8; 3.8 + 1 = 4.8 > 4 → reject. At 11: 3.6 → reject; at 12: 3.2 → reject. At 14: 4 × 0.6 = 2.4 → accept (current becomes 1). At 17: 4 × 0.3 + 1 = 2.2 → accept. At 19: 0.4 + 2 = 2.4 → accept. At 23 (window 2, previous = 3): 3 × 0.7 = 2.1 → accept. Total 8 — the same count as the exact log, from two numbers. It differs in which requests pass: it rejected 11 (which the log allowed) and allowed 14 (which the log rejected), because its "evenly spread" assumption is wrong for a window whose four requests were bunched at the end. Cloudflare measured this approximation on 400 million requests and found 0.003% wrongly allowed or limited.

Token bucket. Capacity 4 tokens, refilled at 0.4 tokens per second (4 per 10 s — the same long-run rate), starting full. Each request needs 1 token. t = 1: 4 → 3. t = 6: 3 + 5 × 0.4 = 5, capped at 4 → 3. t = 8: 3.8 → 2.8. t = 9: 3.2 → 2.2. t = 9.5: 2.4 → 1.4 (accepted — the bucket still holds part of its burst allowance). t = 10.5: 1.8 → 0.8. t = 11: 1.0 → 0. t = 12: 0.4 → reject. t = 14: 1.2 → 0.2. t = 17: 1.4 → 0.4. t = 19: 1.2 → 0.2. t = 23: 1.8 → 0.8. Total 11. The bucket is the most permissive here because it expresses "4 per 10 s" as "a burst of 4, then 0.4 per second", which lets through anything not faster than the drip once the burst is spent. Over a long run its average still converges to 0.4 per second.

Sliding log1 timestamp per request8ExactLow limits that must be exact (login attempts)
Sliding counter2 counters8Nearly exact, smoothPer-minute API limits at scale
