The choice is about what the limit means to the customer. "No more than 1,000 per minute, ever" is a sliding window. "Up to 100 per second sustained, with short bursts allowed" is a token bucket, and it is what most public APIs advertise (Stripe's request-rate limiter is a token bucket; Anthropic's API documents its limits as token buckets). Fixed windows survive where counts must line up with calendar periods.

7 · Deep dive B: shared counters and the race

The naive version. Each gateway does: count = GET key; if count < limit, INCR key and allow; else reject. Every individual Redis command is atomic, but this is two commands with a decision between them. Suppose the limit is 100 and the count is 99. Gateways A and B each receive a request at the same moment. A runs GET → 99. B runs GET → 99. Both decide "under the limit". A runs INCR → 100. B runs INCR → 101. Both requests are allowed. With 50 gateways all receiving requests for a key that is at its limit during a burst, the overshoot can be tens of requests per window. This is the check-then-act race (os4) in a distributed costume.

A better order, and a new race. INCR returns the new value atomically, so "INCR first, then compare" removes the first race: A gets 100 (allowed), B gets 101 (rejected). For a fixed window, the key also needs an expiry so it resets. The Redis documentation's own example does exactly this: INCR key; if the result is 1 (the key was just created), EXPIRE key 1. And it flags the race: if the client crashes, times out or is killed after the INCR but before the EXPIRE, the key exists without an expiry. It never resets. Its count grows past the limit and stays there, and that user is rejected forever — until someone deletes the key by hand. Under load, with timeouts and deploys killing gateway processes mid-request, "rare" happens daily across a fleet.

The atomic fix: one Lua script. Redis runs a Lua script to completion without running any other command in between; its documentation describes the guarantee as all of the script's effects having either not yet happened or already happened. So read, decide and write become one indivisible step, in one network round trip:

-- fixed window: KEYS[1] = counter key, ARGV[1] = limit, ARGV[2] = window seconds
local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2]) end
if n > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end
return 1

A token bucket needs real decision logic — refill by elapsed time, compare, spend — so a script is the natural home for it:

-- token bucket: KEYS[1] = bucket key; ARGV = capacity, refill_per_sec, cost
local cap, rate, cost = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]), tonumber(ARGV[3])
local t = redis.call('TIME')                          -- the store's clock, not the gateway's
local now = tonumber(t[1]) + tonumber(t[2]) / 1e6
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or cap                  -- missing key = full bucket
local ts = tonumber(b[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + math.max(0, now - ts) * rate)
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then tokens = tokens - cost; allowed = 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(cap / rate * 1000))  -- idle until full = forget
return {allowed, tostring(tokens)}

Three details carry the design. The clock comes from Redis's TIME, so every decision for one key uses one timeline; if each gateway passed its own time, a node whose clock ran 200 ms fast would refill buckets early, and the math.max(0, …) guard exists because time can still step backwards after a failover. (Older Redis versions re-ran scripts on replicas, which made reading the clock unsafe; Redis switched to replicating a script's effects by default in 5.0 and exclusively in 7.0.) The expiry is the time to refill from empty to full: after that, a missing key and a full bucket are the same thing, so forgetting it is free. The return value includes the remaining tokens so the gateway can fill rate-limit headers.

Multiple rules in one call. To check "per key per second" and "per key per endpoint per minute" together, the script takes several keys, computes every rule's decision first, and spends from all only if all allow. Redis Cluster requires every key a script touches to be in the same slot, which is what the {k_123} hash tag guarantees.

Without scripts. If scripts are not available (some managed caches restrict them), make each step individually safe: SET key 0 EX 60 NX creates the counter with its expiry in one atomic command if it does not exist, and a following INCR can no longer leak an expiry-less key. Memcache-based designs like Cloudflare's rely on atomic increments on keys that already include the window number, and let the cache's own eviction and expiry clean up.

8 · Deep dive C: local versus global, regions, and failure policy

Purely local. Each gateway enforces limit ÷ N with an in-memory bucket. Zero added latency, no dependency. The problems: (1) uneven traffic — a client using one long-lived HTTP/2 connection lands all its requests on one node and gets only 1/N of its limit; (2) fleet changes — when autoscaling moves N from 20 to 40, every client's effective limit silently halves unless every node learns the new N; (3) burst overshoot — a client spread across all nodes can spend each node's full burst capacity simultaneously.

Purely central. Every check is a round trip to the shard owning the key: accurate (within the algorithm's own approximation), about 0.5 ms in-region, and a dependency on every request. This is what Stripe describes: token buckets in a central Redis.

Hybrids, with the overshoot computed. Periodic sync: each node counts locally and every 100 ms pushes its delta to Redis and pulls the global count. Between syncs, each node decides on stale information. Worked bound: limit 1,000 per minute for a key, 20 nodes, and the key has 50 requests of allowance left. If the client suddenly sends to all 20 nodes, each node believes 50 remain and can allow up to 50 before the next sync — up to 1,000 admitted against 50, a large overshoot for an abusive client. The fix is to give each node only a share: allow at most remaining ÷ N per interval, which over-restricts clients concentrated on one node. Token leasing: a node takes a lease of tokens from the central bucket (say 10% of remaining, at least 1) and spends them locally, returning to Redis only when the lease runs out. Overshoot is bounded by the outstanding leases; round trips drop by the lease size; unused leases are returned or expire. This is the "strip of wristbands" from the primer, and it is the usual answer for very high-rate keys.

ApproachAdded latencyAccuracyStore loadMain risk
Local only0Poor if traffic uneven or N changesNoneWrong limits silently
Central per request~0.5 ms in-regionGood1 call per requestStore is on the hot path
Periodic sync0 on request pathOvershoot ≈ rate × interval × nodesN calls per interval per keyBursts between syncs
Token lease0 for most requestsOvershoot ≤ outstanding leases1 call per leaseLeases stranded on dead nodes

Multiple regions. The estimate already ruled out a synchronous cross-region call per request. Three workable designs: (1) Per-region limits. Split the global limit by each region's traffic share (a customer with 60% of traffic in us-east gets 60% of the limit there); simple and common, but wrong when a client's traffic shifts regions. (2) Local enforcement, asynchronous reconciliation. Each region counts locally and broadcasts its counts every second or so; each region enforces against local count plus the last-known remote counts. The overshoot is bounded by the client's rate in other regions times the sync delay: at 300 requests per second in each of three regions and a 1-second delay, up to 600 extra. Counters that only grow within a window merge cleanly across regions (sum the per-region counts), which is the idea behind a grow-only counter, one of the simplest CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types: structures whose copies can be merged in any order and still agree). (3) Route the client to one place. Cloudflare relies on anycast sending traffic from one IP address to the same data centre under normal conditions, so it counts per data centre and never needs a global counter; the trade-off it accepts is that a client whose traffic is split across locations is counted separately in each.

Fail-open versus fail-closed. When Redis is slow or unreachable, the limiter must decide without its data. Fail open means allow; fail closed means reject. For general API limits, failing closed turns a limiter outage into a total API outage; Stripe states it fails open and accepts that rate limiting is briefly not enforced. The mature version is fail open with a backstop: when the store is unavailable, each gateway falls back to its local bucket at limit ÷ N (or somewhat higher), so a flood is still bounded. For limits whose purpose is to stop abuse that costs real money or security — login attempts (credential stuffing), SMS or email sends (toll fraud), payouts — fail closed, or fall back to a strict local limit. Whatever the policy, the limiter call needs a hard timeout (2-5 ms) and a circuit breaker (sc12), because a limiter that waits 30 seconds for a dead Redis is worse than either policy. Make the policy per rule, as in the data model's fail_mode, and emit a metric for every fallback decision.

9 · Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs

Hot keys. One customer at 100,000 requests per second puts all its checks on one Redis shard. Options: split its counter into k sub-keys with different hash tags, each holding limit ÷ k, and pick a sub-key at random per request; or give that customer leased tokens so most checks are local.

Failover resets. Redis replication is asynchronous; when a primary fails, the replica may be a few milliseconds to seconds behind, so some counters reset or step back. For rate limiting, a brief over-admission after a failover is acceptable — another reason not to use this system for billing-grade quotas, which need durable, exactly-once counting.

Retry storms. Rejected clients that retry immediately multiply the load the limiter sees and keep themselves rejected. Return Retry-After, document backoff with jitter, and consider charging rejected requests a small cost so tight retry loops stay limited.

Rule mistakes. A rule with limit 0, or one whose match pattern accidentally covers every key, is an instant self-inflicted outage. Validate rules, roll them out in shadow mode first, then to a fraction of keys, and keep rollback one click away.

The limiter as a dependency. Each gateway call to Redis is another thing that can be slow. Keep connections pooled, scripts loaded (call by SHA, reload on the "no such script" error after failover), and the timeout tight.

Trade-offs to close on. Accuracy versus latency (central versus local versus leased); exactness versus memory (log versus counters); bursts versus smoothness (token bucket versus sliding window); availability versus protection (fail-open versus fail-closed, chosen per rule); global versus regional (synchronous checks are too slow, so global limits are approximations).
deep:
Stripe's four limiters: rate limiting is one of several layers

Stripe's write-up separates four mechanisms, and the separation is the lesson. A request rate limiter caps each user's requests per second (with bursts allowed) and fires constantly — Stripe says it rejected millions of requests in a month. A concurrent requests limiter caps how many requests a user has in flight (their example is 20), which catches clients hammering expensive endpoints; it fired about 12,000 times in a month. A fleet usage load shedder reserves a share of capacity for critical requests — with a 20% reservation, non-critical traffic above its 80% allocation is rejected. And a worker utilisation load shedder sheds traffic by priority tier when workers are overloaded; it rejected about 100 requests in the month. The first two are per-client fairness; the last two protect the service as a whole regardless of who is sending. An interview answer that only has the first is incomplete.

Concurrency limiting done safely

A counter of in-flight requests (INCR at start, DECR at finish) leaks forever when a request's process dies between the two. The robust form stores request ids: a sorted set per client with each in-flight request's id scored by its start time. On start, a script removes members older than the maximum request duration (cleaning up crashed requests), checks the set's size against the limit, and adds the new id if allowed; on finish, it removes the id. The timeout-based cleanup turns a leak into a bounded delay.

GCRA: one number per key

The generic cell rate algorithm stores, per key, a single timestamp: the "theoretical arrival time" (TAT) of the next request if the client sent at exactly the allowed rate. For a rate of one request per T seconds and a burst tolerance τ, a request at time t is allowed if t ≥ TAT − τ; if allowed, TAT becomes max(TAT, t) + T. It makes the same decisions as a token bucket but needs one value and one comparison, which makes it cheap in a script and easy to expire. ld2 derives it in detail.

Counting in the right unit: tokens for LLM APIs

For an LLM API a request is the wrong unit: one call may process 200 tokens, the next 200,000, and GPU cost scales with tokens. Providers limit requests per minute and tokens per minute, often input and output separately. The difficulty is that output tokens are unknown when the request is admitted. Anthropic's documentation describes one concrete answer: limits on requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute, implemented as token buckets; input tokens estimated at the start of a request and adjusted to the actual count; output tokens counted in real time as they are produced, so the max_tokens parameter does not count against the limit; and, for most models, input tokens read from the prompt cache not counted at all. In a design you build, the general pattern is reserve, then reconcile: charge what you know at admission (input tokens from the tokenizer, plus perhaps an estimate of output), stream the response while charging output as it is generated, and refund or charge the difference at the end. The limiter's script takes a cost argument precisely so this works.

Priorities and fairness inside a limit

Not all requests from one customer are equal: a checkout call matters more than an analytics export. Tiered buckets — separate allowances per priority, or a shared bucket where low-priority requests must leave a reserve of tokens untouched — let a customer's critical traffic keep flowing while their batch jobs are throttled. Across customers, weighted fair sharing of a common capacity (each tenant gets a share proportional to its plan, unused share is lent out) is the multi-tenant version, and is how GPU capacity is often divided on shared inference platforms.

Quotas are a different system

"10 million requests per month, then billing stops you" sounds like a rate limit with a long window, but its requirements are opposite: it must be durable (a Redis failover must not reset a month's usage), exact enough to bill, and auditable. Build it as an append-only usage log aggregated into a database, checked asynchronously with a small allowance of overage, and keep the per-second rate limiter as the fast, approximate, forgetful system it should be.

Adaptive limits

Static limits are guesses. Adaptive systems change the admitted rate from feedback: when backend latency or error rates rise, lower the global admission rate (the way TCP's congestion control backs off), and raise it slowly when healthy. Per-client limits then protect fairness, while the adaptive limit protects the service. The risk is oscillation, so changes are damped and bounded.
prod:
The real cases: Stripe and Cloudflare

Stripe (Paul Tarjan, "Scaling your API with rate limiters", 2017) describes the four limiters above, implemented with the token bucket algorithm on a centralised Redis (or ElastiCache) store. Three operational choices stand out. It fails open: if Redis is unavailable, requests continue, because the limiter should never be the cause of an outage. It dark-launches every limiter, watching the traffic it would have blocked before enforcing. And it returns 429 for rate limiting and 503 for load shedding, so clients can tell "you are sending too much" from "we are overloaded". The write-up also makes the case that rate limiting is a reliability feature for the provider, not a punishment for clients: the request-rate limiter fires constantly, and that is it working.

Cloudflare ("How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains", 2017) faced a different scale: limits configured by millions of customers on traffic arriving at data centres worldwide. Two decisions made it tractable. First, count per data centre: anycast routing normally sends one client IP to the same location, so a per-location counter sees all of that client's traffic, avoiding cross-location coordination and its latency; counters live in a memcache cluster (behind Twemproxy) in each location. Second, the sliding-window counter: two numbers per counter, updated with atomic increments and no transactions. Its worked example — 42 requests in the previous minute, 18 so far in the current one, 15 seconds in — estimates 42 × 0.75 + 18 = 49.5 requests against a limit of 50. Measured on 400 million requests from 270,000 sources, only 0.003% were wrongly allowed or limited, with an average 6% difference between the real and approximate rates.

Put side by side, the two cases show the axis interviewers want you to reason along: Stripe needs per-customer correctness across a fleet in a few regions and centralises in Redis; Cloudflare needs global scale and pushes counting to the edge, trading cross-location accuracy for latency and availability.

Failure modes you will see

The permanently blocked user. Symptom: one key rejected forever after a deploy. Cause: a counter created without an expiry (the INCR-then-EXPIRE race). Detection: alert on limiter keys with no TTL (TTL key returns −1). Fix: atomic scripts, plus a sweeper for the existing bad keys.

Silent fail-open. Symptom: an abusive client is not limited during an incident. Cause: Redis timeouts triggering fail-open without anyone noticing. Detection: a metric and alert on fallback decisions.

Limits halving after autoscaling. Symptom: customers complain of 429s at half their contracted rate. Cause: local limits computed as limit ÷ N with a stale or new N. Fix: central counting, or nodes that learn N from the fleet registry.

Hot shard. Symptom: p99 limiter latency rises on one Redis shard. Cause: one large customer or a scraping IP. Fix: split the key or lease tokens.

What to monitor

Decisions per second by rule and outcome; top limited keys; limiter call latency (p50/p99) and timeout rate; fallback (fail-open/closed) decisions; Redis CPU and memory per shard; keys without TTL; shadow-mode would-reject counts before every rule rollout; and, from the client side, 429 rate per customer, since a sudden rise usually means a client bug, not an attack.
myths: Redis INCR is atomic, so any limiter built on it is race-free.

Each Redis command is atomic on its own, but a limiter usually needs several steps: read a value, decide, increment, set an expiry. A GET followed by INCR lets two gateways both read 99 against a limit of 100 and both allow; an INCR followed by a separate EXPIRE can leave a counter with no expiry if the client dies in between, blocking that user forever. Put the whole decision in one Lua script, or design the steps so each one is safe on its own.
Splitting the global limit evenly across gateway nodes is equivalent to a global limit.

Only if traffic is spread evenly, which it rarely is. A client holding one long-lived HTTP/2 connection lands on one node and gets only 1/N of its limit; a client spread across all nodes at once can get its full limit on each node during a burst. And N changes every time the fleet autoscales.
A rate limiter should fail closed, because letting traffic through defeats its purpose.

For general API limits the limiter protects capacity, and a limiter outage that rejects every request is a full outage caused by the protection layer. Stripe fails open and relies on other defences. Fail closed only where a single allowed request is expensive or dangerous (login attempts, SMS sends, payouts), and even then prefer a strict local fallback to rejecting everything.
The sliding-window log is the best algorithm because it is exact.

It is exact and it stores a timestamp for every accepted request in the window. At 1,000 requests per minute per key that is up to 1,000 entries per key — tens of kilobytes — and millions of keys make it hundreds of gigabytes. Cloudflare measured its two-counter approximation wrong on only 0.003% of 400 million requests. Exactness is rarely worth that memory.
Rate limiting is only about requests per second.

Requests differ in cost. An LLM API limits input and output tokens per minute as well as requests, a search API may weight expensive queries more, and long streaming requests need a concurrency limit. The limiter must accept a cost per request, and sometimes reconcile it after the request finishes.
lab:
Goal: replay the four algorithms on the lesson's request trace, then reproduce the check-then-act race with threads and fix it with an atomic step. Python 3.12 standard library, a few seconds.

"""Four rate limiters on one trace, then the GET-then-INCR race vs an atomic check."""
import threading, time

LIMIT, WIN = 4, 10.0
TRACE = [1, 6, 8, 9, 9.5, 10.5, 11, 12, 14, 17, 19, 23]

def fixed(ts):
    counts, out = {}, []
    for t in ts:
        w = int(t // WIN); ok = counts.get(w, 0) < LIMIT
        if ok: counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
        out.append(ok)
    return out

def sliding_log(ts):
    log, out = [], []
    for t in ts:
        log = [a for a in log if a > t - WIN]; ok = len(log) < LIMIT
        if ok: log.append(t)
        out.append(ok)
    return out

def sliding_counter(ts):
    counts, out = {}, []
    for t in ts:
        w = int(t // WIN)
        est = counts.get(w - 1, 0) * (WIN - (t - w * WIN)) / WIN + counts.get(w, 0)
        ok = est + 1 <= LIMIT
        if ok: counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
        out.append(ok)
    return out

def token_bucket(ts, cap=4, rate=0.4):
    tokens, last, out = cap, 0.0, []
    for t in ts:
        tokens = min(cap, tokens + (t - last) * rate); last = t
        ok = tokens >= 1 - 1e-9                       # tolerate float rounding
        if ok: tokens -= 1
        out.append(ok)
    return out

for fn in (fixed, sliding_log, sliding_counter, token_bucket):
    res = fn(TRACE)
    print(f"{fn.__name__:>16}: " + " ".join("✓" if r else "✗" for r in res) + f"  ({sum(res)} allowed)")

# --- the race: 50 gateways, one key at its last 10 units of allowance -------------
store, lock = {"k": 90}, threading.Lock()              # the lock stands in for Redis's single thread

def naive(results):                                    # GET, think, INCR: three separate steps
    seen = store["k"]; time.sleep(0.002)               # network hop + gateway logic
    if seen < 100:
        with lock: store["k"] += 1
        results.append(True)

def atomic(results):                                   # what one Lua script does
    with lock:
        if store["k"] < 100: store["k"] += 1; results.append(True)

for fn in (naive, atomic):
    store["k"], results = 90, []
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=fn, args=(results,)) for _ in range(50)]
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()
    print(f"{fn.__name__:>6}: allowed {len(results)} with 10 remaining; counter ends at {store['k']}")
  1. The first block should print 9, 8, 8 and 11 allowed — the same marks as the timeline figure. Change TRACE to put 4 requests at t = 9.1-9.9 and 4 at t = 10.1-10.9 and watch the fixed window let all 8 through.
  2. The race block: the naive version typically allows far more than 10 (often all 50), because every thread reads 90 before any write lands; the atomic version allows exactly 10 and the counter ends at 100.
  3. Set the token bucket's rate to 0.1 and cap to 1: it becomes a strict "one per 10 s" limiter. Then try cap=8, rate=0.4 to see how capacity controls burst size independently of the long-run rate.
recap: A distributed rate limiter is a decision service consulted on every request: given a key and a cost, allow or reject, fast and without becoming the outage itself.

Fixed windows allow up to twice the limit across a boundary; a sliding-window log is exact but stores every timestamp; a sliding-window counter weights the previous window and is nearly exact with two numbers; a token bucket allows a burst up to its capacity and refills at a steady rate.
Shared counters live in a store like Redis, sharded by key, with all keys for one client hashed to the same shard so one script can update them together.
Check-then-act (GET then INCR) overshoots under concurrency, and INCR then a separate EXPIRE can leak a counter with no expiry; one Lua script makes read-decide-write atomic in one round trip.
Using the store's clock (Redis TIME) inside the script avoids clock skew between gateway nodes.
Purely local limits are fast but inaccurate when traffic is uneven or the fleet size changes; global limits are accurate but add a network hop; hybrids sync or lease tokens and bound the overshoot.
Multi-region limits are usually enforced per region, with the global limit split by traffic share or reconciled asynchronously, because a cross-region round trip per request is too slow.
General API limiters fail open with a local backstop; security-critical limiters fail closed; either way the limiter call has a tight timeout.
Stripe runs request-rate and concurrency limiters plus two load shedders, all token buckets in Redis, and dark-launches each one; Cloudflare counts per data centre with a sliding-window counter.
For LLM APIs the unit is tokens: input tokens are known at admission, output tokens are counted as they are generated, so admission uses an estimate and reconciles afterwards.
glossary: The HTTP status code for a rejected rate-limited request, defined in RFC 6585; it may carry a Retry-After header.
Done as one indivisible step, so no other operation can observe or interleave with a half-finished state.
A bug where a value is read, a decision is made, and a write follows in a separate step, so a concurrent writer can invalidate the decision in between.

Running a new limiter so it records what it would have rejected without actually rejecting anything.
A key-value pair describing a request (API key, route, IP) that rules match against to choose a limit.
Rejecting requests when the limiter cannot decide, for example because its store is down.
Allowing requests when the limiter cannot decide.

Rejecting work because the server is overloaded, independent of which client sent it.

drill:
Work it out

Your API gateway fleet has 40 nodes behind a round-robin load balancer. A customer's contract says 2,000 requests per minute. Today each node runs a local token bucket of 50 per minute (2,000 ÷ 40). (a) The customer's SDK uses 4 long-lived HTTP/2 connections. What rate do they actually get? (b) Autoscaling takes the fleet to 80 nodes for a sale and nobody updates the bucket size. Now what? (c) Propose a design and estimate its Redis load if the customer sends at their full limit and 5,000 other customers average 300 per minute.

Answer

(a) HTTP/2 multiplexes all requests over a connection, and a connection-level load balancer pins each connection to one node. Four connections reach at most 4 nodes, each allowing 50 per minute: 200 per minute, a tenth of the contract. The customer sees 429s at 10% of their limit and files a ticket — a correct "limit" configured in a way that is wrong for real traffic.

(b) With 80 nodes, a client spread evenly across all nodes could get 80 × 50 = 4,000 per minute, twice the contract, while the pinned customer still gets 200. Local limits are wrong in both directions depending on traffic shape and fleet size.

(c) Central token buckets in Redis, one script call per request: the customer at 2,000 per minute is 33 calls per second; 5,000 others at 300 per minute is 5,000 × 5 = 25,000 calls per second. Total about 25,000 calls per second — within one shard's capacity at the 50,000 planning figure, but use 3 shards with replicas for headroom and failure tolerance. Keep a local bucket per node at 2,000 ÷ N × 2 as a fail-open backstop. If one customer later grows to 100,000 per minute, lease tokens to nodes in batches of, say, 20 to cut its Redis calls by 20× with overshoot bounded by 40 nodes × 20 = 800 tokens.

Diagnose it

After a gateway deploy, a handful of customers are rejected on every request with "100 requests/second exceeded", even when they send one request per minute. Other customers are fine. Redis shows their counter keys with values in the tens of thousands. What happened and what do you change?

Answer

Their counter keys have no expiry. The limiter runs INCR and, if the result is 1, a separate EXPIRE. During the deploy, gateway processes were killed between those two commands for a few keys, so those keys were created without a TTL. They never reset; every request increments them further; the comparison fails forever. Confirm with TTL key, which returns −1 (no expiry) for the affected keys. Immediate fix: delete or set expiries on keys with no TTL. Real fix: make creation and expiry atomic — a Lua script that does INCR and EXPIRE together, or SET key 0 EX 1 NX before INCR — and add an alert on limiter keys without a TTL. The general lesson: in a distributed limiter, every multi-step update is a race the next deploy will find.
qa: E
Why does a rate limiter for a fleet of gateways need shared state?

Because a client's requests are spread across many gateway nodes by the load balancer, and each node alone only sees its share. To enforce '100 per minute for this API key', someone must count all of that key's requests, which means a shared counter (or nodes that exchange counts). The design question is how to share it without adding much latency or a single point of failure.
E
Compare fixed window and token bucket.

A fixed window counts requests per calendar interval and resets at the boundary, so a client can send the full limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next — twice the limit in a short span. A token bucket holds up to a capacity of tokens refilled at a steady rate; it allows a burst up to the capacity and then a smooth rate, with no boundary effect. Both need only two numbers per key.
Follow-up: When is fixed window fine? — For long-period quotas (requests per day) where boundary bursts do not hurt, and when you want counts that line up with billing periods.
E
What should a rate-limited client see?

HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header saying when to try again, and headers on every response showing the limit, the remaining allowance and when it resets, so well-behaved clients can slow down before being rejected. The error body should say which limit was hit. Clients should back off with jitter rather than retrying immediately.
M
What is the race in a naive Redis limiter, and how do you fix it?

Two races. GET-then-INCR lets concurrent gateways read the same count below the limit and all proceed, overshooting. INCR then EXPIRE as separate calls means a client that crashes between them leaves a counter with no expiry, which grows past the limit and blocks the user permanently. Fix both by running the logic in one Lua script, which Redis executes atomically, or by structuring it so each step is safe alone (SET with NX and EX to create the key with its expiry, then INCR).

Follow-up: Does MULTI/EXEC work too? — It makes INCR and EXPIRE execute together, but it cannot branch on a value read inside the transaction, so decision logic like a token bucket still needs a script.
M
Why read the time inside the Redis script rather than pass it from the gateway?

Gateway nodes' clocks differ by milliseconds or more. If each node passes its own 'now', a node with a fast clock refills buckets early and a slow one can make time go backwards for a key, producing negative refills or extra tokens. Using the store's clock gives every decision for a key one consistent timeline. Modern Redis replicates script effects rather than re-running scripts, so calling TIME in a script is safe.
Follow-up: What if the Redis primary fails over? — The new primary's clock may differ slightly; refill computation should clamp negative elapsed time to zero.
M
How do you size the Redis cluster for 500,000 API requests per second?

One script call per request (all rules for a key in one script), so 500,000 calls per second. Assume a conservative 50,000 script calls per second per shard: 10 primaries, 15-20 with headroom, each with a replica. Memory is small: 10 million active keys × 3 rules × about 100 bytes is 3 GB. The binding constraint is per-shard CPU and hot keys, not memory.
Follow-up: What about one customer sending 100,000 requests per second? — That key lives on one shard; split it into sub-counters across shards, or enforce part of its limit locally on each gateway.
M
Local limits or a central store: how do you choose?

Central gives an accurate global count at the cost of a network hop (sub-millisecond in a region) and a dependency. Local gives zero added latency but each node sees only part of the traffic, so you split the limit by node count, which is wrong when traffic is uneven or the fleet scales. Most systems use central counters for per-customer limits and local token buckets as a coarse first line and fallback.
Follow-up: How do you reduce central calls? — Batch: let a node take a lease of tokens, or sync counts every 100 ms, accepting a bounded overshoot.
M
Should the limiter fail open or closed when Redis is unavailable?

It depends on what an extra request costs. General API rate limits fail open — a limiter outage should not become an API outage — with a local per-node token bucket as a backstop so a flood is still bounded. Limits that defend against abuse where each request has a real cost (login attempts, SMS sends, payouts) fail closed or fall back to a strict local limit. Either way, the limiter call has a tight timeout (a few milliseconds) and a circuit breaker.
Follow-up: How would you know the fallback is working? — Emit a metric for every fail-open decision and alert on it; dark-launch the fallback path regularly.
M
How do you change limits safely?

Treat rules as configuration with versioning and staged rollout. Deploy a new or tighter rule in shadow mode first, logging what it would reject, and compare against expectations; then enforce for a fraction of keys; then everywhere. Validate rules before pushing (a limit of zero, or a typo matching every key, is an instant outage). Stripe recommends dark-launching each limiter for exactly this reason.
H
How do you enforce a global limit across three regions?

Avoid a synchronous cross-region call per request; it adds 50-150 ms. Either split the limit statically by each region's traffic share (simple, but a client that moves regions sees a smaller limit), or enforce locally and exchange counts asynchronously every second or so, accepting overshoot of up to the client's rate times the sync delay in each other region. Some providers route a client consistently to one region or data centre (Cloudflare relies on anycast to send one IP to the same location) so counting can stay local.

Follow-up: What is the overshoot bound for async sync? — Roughly (regions − 1) × per-region rate × sync interval; at 300 requests per second per region, three regions and 1 s sync, up to 600 extra requests.
H
Design a concurrency limiter for long-running requests.

Rate limits do not bound how many requests are in flight; long streams can pile up. Keep a sorted set per client in Redis with in-flight request ids scored by start time. On start, a script removes entries older than a timeout (crashed requests that never finished), checks the set size against the limit, and adds the id if allowed. On finish, remove the id. The timeout cleanup is essential, because without it a crash leaks a slot forever.
Follow-up: Why not a simple counter with INCR and DECR? — A crash between start and finish leaks an increment forever; ids with timestamps can be expired.
H
How would you rate-limit an LLM API by tokens rather than requests?

Use separate token buckets for requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute. Input tokens are known at admission (count them with the tokenizer) and can be charged up front; output tokens are unknown, so either charge them as they are generated during streaming or reserve an estimate and refund the difference at the end. Anthropic's API documents this shape: requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute with a token bucket, input tokens estimated at the start and adjusted, output tokens counted as they are produced, and cached input tokens not counted for most models.

Follow-up: Why not charge max_tokens up front? — It over-reserves badly (most responses are far shorter than the maximum), so clients would hit limits while capacity sits idle; charging actual output avoids that.
H
How would this change if an ML model were in the path, for example to decide limits?

An abuse model can score each client and adjust its bucket size or put it in a stricter tier, but the model must stay off the per-request hot path: score asynchronously from logs and write the resulting tier into the rules store, so the limiter itself still does a constant-time check. Keep hard caps the model cannot exceed, log its decisions for review, and roll out changes in shadow mode like any other rule.

Follow-up: What goes wrong with a model setting limits? — Feedback loops: limiting a client changes its traffic, which changes its features. Evaluate against held-out decisions, not just the model's own outputs.

t: Design Instagram / photo sharing (upload, storage, feed, media delivery)
sum: The media half of a social app: resumable uploads straight to object storage with pre-signed URLs, a resize pipeline and the storage maths per photo, Haystack-style blob storage, CDN hit ratio and egress cost, and serving a celebrity's post to a hundred million phones.
prereq: cd3
A news feed is built by fan-out on write (push post ids into followers' timelines), fan-out on read, or a hybrid with special handling for accounts with millions of followers.
in7
Object storage keeps immutable blobs under keys, replicated or erasure-coded across disks and racks, with metadata in a separate index.
net12
A CDN caches content at edge locations near users; the hit ratio decides origin load, and tiered caching puts a shield layer between edges and the origin.
cd4
Video services pre-encode many renditions of each upload and serve them from CDNs; egress bytes, not compute, dominate the bill.
sc10
A durable queue decouples a fast producer from slow workers, so uploads are accepted at once and processed asynchronously with retries.
cd6
Large files are uploaded in chunks so a failure retries one chunk, not the whole file, and content hashes allow deduplication.
why:
A woman at a concert takes a photo on her phone, picks a filter, types a caption and taps Share. The venue's mobile network is overloaded; the upload stalls at 60%, drops, and resumes when she walks outside. Within a second of the upload finishing, the photo is in her followers' feeds as a crisp image on a large phone, a small thumbnail on her profile grid, and a medium image in a friend's browser in another continent. A year later, someone scrolls back to it and it still loads instantly. Meanwhile, the band she was watching posts their own photo of the crowd, and 40 million people see it within the hour.

The feed side of this — deciding which posts each person sees and pushing post ids into timelines — is the news-feed problem from cd3. This lesson is about the other half, which is where most of the bytes, the cost and the engineering live: getting a multi-megabyte file off an unreliable phone connection; turning it into the handful of sizes and formats that phones actually display; storing hundreds of terabytes of new images every day for years without paying for disk seeks you do not need; and delivering hundreds of thousands of images per second to phones all over the world, where the bill is measured in petabytes of egress.

Each of those breaks a naive design. Uploading through the application servers ties them up streaming bytes. Resizing on demand repeats the same CPU work millions of times. Storing each photo as a file in a normal file system costs several disk operations per read, which Facebook found to be the bottleneck of its first photo store. And a CDN, which seems to solve reads, still leaves a long tail of older photos that miss the cache and a stampede problem for the hottest ones.

This lesson follows the interview flow: requirements; estimates done by hand (upload rate and bandwidth, storage per photo and per year, image fetches per second, egress and its cost, cache size); API and data model; the high-level design with the upload and read paths; then three deep dives — uploads (pre-signed URLs, resumable and multipart uploads), the processing pipeline and the storage maths per photo, and delivery (CDN hit ratio, egress cost, and the hot celebrity post). The real case is Facebook's Haystack paper, which describes a photo store built for exactly this workload, and its successor f4 for photos that have gone cold. The lab is a calculator for storage and egress that you can point at your own assumptions.
primer:
The mental model: a photo lab with a mail-order catalogue

Think of an old-fashioned photo lab that serves a whole country by mail. Customers do not hand film to the shop owner at the counter; they drop it in a dedicated post box that goes straight to the lab's loading dock (the owner just gives them a numbered envelope). In the darkroom, every roll is developed once and printed at a fixed set of sizes — wallet, postcard, poster — because printing on demand for every request would keep the darkroom busy forever. Prints go into a warehouse organised for fast retrieval, not into a filing cabinet where every request means opening three drawers. And copies of popular prints are stocked in local shops in every town, so most customers never touch the warehouse at all.

The numbered envelope is a pre-signed URL: permission to deliver exactly one item to exactly one place, valid for a short time. The post box straight to the dock is the direct upload to object storage, bypassing the API servers. The darkroom is the asynchronous processing pipeline that generates derivatives — fixed sizes and formats. The warehouse is blob storage designed for one disk read per photo. The local shops are the CDN. And the shop owner at the counter is the metadata service: small records about who posted what, when, with which caption and which stored sizes.

The analogy breaks in instructive ways. A real lab ships each print once; a popular photo here is fetched millions of times, and each local shop has to fetch its first copy from the warehouse — if a thousand shops all ask at the same second, the warehouse is swamped. And mail is slow, so nobody minds waiting; here the user expects to see their own photo posted instantly, which is achieved by showing it from the phone's local copy while the lab catches up.

Two paths that share almost nothing

The most useful single observation in this design is that metadata and media have opposite shapes. Metadata — users, posts, follows, likes, comments, and the list of stored variants for each photo — is small (hundreds of bytes per record), changes constantly, needs transactions and indexes, and lives in sharded databases with caches in front. Media — the image bytes — is large (kilobytes to megabytes per object), never changes once written (an edit creates a new object), needs no queries beyond "get this key", and lives in object storage behind CDNs. Treat them separately and each becomes a well-understood problem; mix them (bytes in the database, or metadata queries against blob storage) and both suffer.

The hour, in order

In the interview, state the split in the first five minutes so the interviewer knows you will not spend the hour on feed ranking. Size the media path in the estimates — that is where the impressive numbers are. Then spend the deep dives on upload, processing and storage, and delivery, and say explicitly that fan-out follows cd3's hybrid design.
body:
0–5Requirements
5–12Estimates
12–20API & data
20–28Architecture
28–48Deep dives
48–56Failures
56–60Close

1 · Requirements

Functional. (1) Upload a photo (or a few in a carousel) with a caption; the upload survives flaky networks. (2) View a home feed of posts from accounts you follow, with images at the right size for the screen. (3) View a profile grid of thumbnails. (4) Like and comment. (5) Delete a post, after which it disappears for everyone. Out of scope, said aloud: video and stories (cd4 covers video delivery), direct messages (cd2), search, ads, and feed ranking (cd3).

Non-functional. Uploads are durable once acknowledged — never lose a photo. A post appears to its author immediately and to followers within seconds. Feed images load fast worldwide: the first image visible in well under a second on a mobile network, which means they come from a CDN edge near the user. High availability for reads; uploads may queue during incidents but must not be lost. Storage and delivery cost matter at this scale and are an explicit requirement. Location metadata in photos must not leak.

Clarifying questions. How many daily users and uploads? Do we keep originals at full resolution? Which screen sizes and formats must we serve? Is there a regional or legal requirement on where photos are stored? How fast must a deletion take effect everywhere?

2 · Back-of-envelope estimates

Assumptions, stated: 500 million daily active users (DAU), 100 million photo uploads per day, each user views about 100 images a day while scrolling, an original averages 3 MB (a modern phone JPEG or HEIC), and peak traffic is 3× average. A day is 86,400 seconds.

Upload rate. 100,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1,160 uploads per second on average, about 3,500 per second at peak. For comparison, Facebook's Haystack paper reported one billion new photos a week in 2010 — about 1,650 per second on average — so these numbers are realistic for a large service.

Upload bandwidth. 3,500 per second × 3 MB = 10.5 GB/s ≈ 84 Gbit/s of ingest at peak. That is why the bytes must not pass through API servers: it would take a fleet of servers doing nothing but relaying bytes.

Derivative sizes. Choose a ladder of four widths, each a JPEG at a sensible quality: a 150 × 150 grid thumbnail (~10 KB), 320 px (~30 KB), 640 px (~80 KB) and 1,080 px (~200 KB). That is 320 KB per photo. Add WebP copies for clients that accept them; Google reports lossy WebP is 25-34% smaller than comparable JPEG, so call it 70% of the JPEG size: 224 KB. Total derivatives ≈ 544 KB per photo.

Storage per day and year. Derivatives: 100M × 544 KB = 54 TB per day, about 20 PB per year; with three full copies, 60 PB. Originals: 100M × 3 MB = 300 TB per day, about 110 PB per year — over five times the derivatives. With three copies, 330 PB a year; with erasure coding at 1.4× (explained in the deep dive), 153 PB. That single number forces a product question: do we keep originals at all?

Image fetches. 500M × 100 = 50 billion image fetches per day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 580,000 per second average, about 1.7 million per second at peak. (Haystack's 2010 paper reported over one million images per second at peak — the same order.)

Egress. Most fetches are the feed sizes; assume an average of 150 KB per fetch. 580,000 × 150 KB ≈ 87 GB/s ≈ 700 Gbit/s average, about 2 Tbit/s at peak; per day, 50 billion × 150 KB = 7.5 PB. At an assumed blended CDN price of $0.01 per GB, that is 7.5 million GB × $0.01 = $75,000 per day, about $27 million a year. Every 10% cut in bytes per image is worth about $2.7 million a year.

Origin load. With a 90% CDN hit ratio, origin storage serves 10%: about 58,000 requests per second and 750 TB per day. At 95%, half that. The Haystack paper reports that roughly 10% of photo requests from CDNs reached its storage layer, consistent with this assumption.

Processing compute. Decoding a 12-megapixel image and producing four resized JPEGs takes on the order of 100-200 ms of CPU; call it 0.2 core-seconds. At 3,500 uploads per second: about 700 cores at peak, before WebP and before any ML moderation. AVIF encoding is several times slower again, which is why it is usually done later and selectively.

Hot cache size. Most views are of recent posts. Two days of uploads at about 320 KB of JPEG derivatives each is 200M × 320 KB ≈ 64 TB — the working set the CDN as a whole must hold, split across edge locations by what each region views.
