8 · Deep dive C: reservations, timeouts and payment

The reservation lifecycle. A reservation is a small state machine: RESERVED → PAID, RESERVED → EXPIRED, RESERVED → CANCELLED. Each transition is a conditional UPDATE on the current state: UPDATE reservations SET status = 'PAID' WHERE id = ? AND status = 'RESERVED'. If two transitions race — the sweeper expiring a hold at the very moment payment confirms — only one finds the row in RESERVED and the other's row count is 0. That makes the outcome exactly one of the three, never two.

How long a hold lasts. Long enough to pay (typing card details, a 3-D Secure bank challenge), short enough that abandoned units come back while demand is still there. Ten minutes is common; some sales use 5. Show the countdown so shoppers know.

Releasing expired holds. Two mechanisms, used together. Active: a sweeper runs every few seconds — UPDATE reservations SET status = 'EXPIRED' WHERE status = 'RESERVED' AND expires_at < now() RETURNING sku, qty — and increments inventory by the returned quantities in the same transaction (or a Redis sorted set scored by expiry time, or a delay queue message per hold, triggers the same transition). Lazy: when a reservation request finds stock at zero, it can expire overdue holds first, so returned units are available immediately even if the sweeper is behind. Either way the unit goes back by the same conditional transition, so it cannot be returned twice.

The payment race. Payment may complete after the hold expired: the shopper paid at 9:59 of a 10-minute hold and the processor took 3 seconds. Prevent most of these with a payment-in-progress state: checkout moves the reservation to PAYING (conditional on RESERVED and not expired) before calling the processor, and the sweeper does not expire PAYING holds until a longer deadline. If payment fails, PAYING returns to RESERVED (or EXPIRED if past time). If the processor confirms after the unit was genuinely lost, void the authorisation automatically.

Authorise now, capture later. Card payments have two steps: authorisation asks the issuer to reserve the amount on the card, and capture actually charges it, often when the item ships. Authorising at checkout means a reservation that is lost to a race, or an order that fails fraud review, can be released by voiding the authorisation, without a refund appearing on the customer's statement. For the sale, the order is confirmed on successful authorisation.

Idempotency end to end. The client generates one idempotency key per checkout attempt and resends it on every retry. The server records the key, a hash of the request and the final response in the same transaction as the order, so a retry returns the stored response instead of charging again; a retry with the same key but a different body is rejected. The call to the payment processor carries its own idempotency key derived from the order id, so a network timeout followed by a retry cannot create a second charge at the processor. A timeout is treated as unknown (cd9): poll the processor or wait for its webhook, never assume failure and charge again. This is the mechanism that would have prevented the 412 double charges in the opening story.

Keep the transaction short. The order transaction does: transition reservation to PAID, insert the order, insert the idempotency record. Emails, fulfilment requests, loyalty points and analytics go to a queue processed afterwards. Every extra write inside the transaction is time the hot rows stay locked during the sale's busiest seconds.

9 · Bot defence and graceful degradation

Bots. Automated buyers win races because they are faster and more numerous. The design response is to make speed and numbers useless: limit units per account, per payment card, per shipping address and per device (enforced with unique constraints and Redis SET NX keys); require accounts to exist and be verified before the sale (new accounts created in the last hour are a strong signal); apply challenges — a CAPTCHA, or a small proof-of-work computation that costs a human nothing but costs a bot farm a lot — at the queue entrance rather than at checkout, where they would slow legitimate buyers at the worst moment; bind admission tokens to the session so they cannot be traded; and score sessions on behaviour and device signals. Randomising the queue position of everyone who arrives before the start removes the reward for millisecond timing. After the sale, cancel orders that violate limits (several accounts shipping to one address) before capture, which is another reason to authorise rather than charge.

Degrade on purpose. Decide in advance what to switch off, in order, and build each switch as a feature flag: personalised recommendations, reviews, "customers also bought", live stock counters, search suggestions, wishlists. Serve the product page as a static, CDN-cached page with the sale state embedded and refreshed every second or two. Shed browse traffic before checkout traffic: an admitted user mid-payment is worth protecting above everything else. Move non-critical writes (analytics events, view counts) to a queue that can lag by minutes. And serve "sold out" as a first-class cached page — the cheapest response to the most common outcome.

10 · Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs

The hot row or key. All reservations hit one SKU's counter; the admission rate must stay below its ceiling, or the counter must move to Redis or be sharded. Watch lock wait time on that row.

Redis and database drift. Decrements in Redis without matching reservations (a crash between the two writes) make Redis report sold out while units remain. The reconciler corrects it; alert when the difference exceeds a few units.

Retry storms. Slow responses cause client retries, which add load, which slows responses. Idempotency makes retries harmless to correctness; Retry-After hints, exponential backoff with jitter in the client and the waiting room's controller make them harmless to capacity.

Payment provider limits. A payment processor applies its own rate limits; a thousand authorisations per second may exceed them. Agree on capacity in advance, and let the admission controller watch payment latency as one of its inputs.

Trade-offs to close on. Durability versus throughput for the counter (database row versus Redis versus shards); fairness versus simplicity (lottery versus first-come); short holds (fewer stranded units) versus long holds (fewer frustrated payers); strict per-customer limits (fewer bots) versus friction for real customers; and the general principle that the sale is decided at admission control, not by adding servers.
deep:
The two-tier counter, done carefully

"Redis gates, the database records" needs an exact protocol, or it leaks units in both directions. Step 1: DECR (or a Lua check-and-decrement) on the Redis counter; if the result is negative, increment back and return sold out. Step 2: in a database transaction, insert the reservation (unique per customer) and decrement the database's available with a conditional UPDATE. Step 3: if step 2 fails for any reason — duplicate customer, database says zero, timeout — increment Redis back. A crash between step 1 and step 2 leaks a unit in Redis (too low); a Redis failover after step 1 may forget the decrement (too high). Neither breaks the guarantee that matters, because the database's conditional UPDATE is the final word — Redis only filters out the obvious losers cheaply. The reconciler then sets Redis to the database's truth every few seconds. The pattern generalises: a fast, approximate gate in front of a slow, exact check, with periodic correction.

Why the database row is slower than it looks

A single-statement conditional UPDATE in autocommit mode holds the row lock from the moment it acquires it until the commit's log record is durable. On a database that flushes its write-ahead log to disk on every commit, that is at least one disk flush — tens to hundreds of microseconds on NVMe, milliseconds on networked storage — during which every other decrement for the SKU waits. Group commit (the database flushing many transactions' log records together) helps total throughput but not one row's serial chain. That is why the ceiling is "about a thousand per second" rather than the hundreds of thousands of simple updates a database can do across many rows. Put the reservation insert in the same transaction and the lock is held slightly longer; put an external call (payment) inside it and the ceiling collapses to the external call's rate — never do that.

Pre-allocation instead of contention

Another way to remove the hot counter is to decide allocations before the sale. A lottery collects registrations for a day, draws 10,000 winners (plus a waitlist), and gives each a time-limited purchase link: the sale becomes 10,000 uncontended checkouts spread over hours. A token pool pre-creates one token per unit and has each admitted user pop one; a per-node allocation gives each reservation server a block of units to sell locally and lets it ask for more when it runs low, the inventory version of leased rate-limit tokens (cd12). Each removes contention by moving coordination to a moment when nobody is waiting.

Multi-SKU carts and bundles

A sale with sizes or colours is many SKUs, and a cart may hold several. Reserving them one at a time risks holding size 9 while size 10 is sold out, then releasing it. Two clean approaches: reserve all the cart's SKUs in one database transaction (conditional UPDATEs on each row, in a fixed order — for example sorted by SKU id — so two carts cannot deadlock by locking the same rows in opposite orders); or in Redis, one Lua script that checks every counter and decrements all only if all are available, with the counters sharing a hash tag so they live on one shard. Either way the reservation is all-or-nothing.

Multi-region sales

A global sale with buyers on three continents cannot afford a cross-region round trip per decrement. Split the stock in advance by expected demand (say 5,000 / 3,000 / 2,000), let each region sell its share locally, and run a coordinator that moves unsold units from slow regions to fast ones every few seconds. The sum across regions never exceeds the total because units are moved, not copied: the coordinator decrements one region's counter before incrementing another's. This is a sharded counter whose shards are regions.

Fairness has measurable definitions

"Fair" can be measured: the spread of queue wait times for users who joined at the same moment (Shopify's metric — median and 95th percentile converging), the share of units bought by accounts flagged as automated, the number of units per shipping address, and the proportion of buyers who were early registrants. Choose the definition before the sale, publish the rule (first-come, random draw, or registered first), and report against it afterwards; customers forgive "sold out" far more readily than they forgive "the bots got it".
prod:
The real case: Shopify's flash sales

Shopify's 2017 engineering write-up (Emil Stolarsky, in two parts) is a first-party account of flash sales hurting a multi-tenant platform. Some merchants ran drops that sold out in minutes, regularly — the post likens it to Black Friday every week or so — and in February 2016 one such sale took down not only that store but every store sharing its database shard. The bottleneck was checkout's writes: each checkout created a record and every step modified it. The first defence was a checkout throttle at the edge: Nginx with OpenResty's Lua module ran a leaky bucket allowing a fixed number of checkout requests per 5-second period, sized to what the application could handle; excess users were sent to a queue page in the merchant's own design (cached by Nginx) rather than shown an error, which polled until let through; admitted users got a signed cookie so they skipped the throttle for the rest of their session. Its flaw was fairness: polling made admission random, and some shoppers waited about as long as the sale lasted.

Part II made the queue fair without central state. Each user's first checkout attempt gets a timestamp in a signed cookie; each load balancer computes its own cutoff time, a virtual "now serving" counter; requests timestamped before the cutoff pass to the leaky bucket. The cutoff moves under a controller borrowed from control theory — after MATLAB simulations of PID controllers, only the proportional term was kept, driven by the bucket's limit minus the requests already passed. The reported result was that median and 95th-percentile queue times converged, and complaints about long or unfair waits stopped at the next big sale. The lesson for interviews: the fairest, most scalable queue here was not a queue data structure at all, but a signed timestamp and a moving threshold.

Failure modes you will see

The site falls over at T+0. Symptom: 5xx errors and timeouts across the store. Cause: the arrival spike reached the origin because the sale page was not cacheable (personalised HTML, a cookie that bypassed the CDN) or the waiting room was not enabled in time. Detection: origin request rate versus CDN hit rate in the first seconds. Prevention: a pre-sale checklist and a load test of the exact configuration.

Oversold. Symptom: orders exceed stock. Cause: a code path that decrements outside the atomic check (an admin tool, a mobile API version, a retry path that re-creates a reservation). Detection: a continuous invariant check — sold + active holds ≤ total — alerting on violation. Prevention: all decrements through one function, database constraints as backstop.

Undersold. Symptom: "sold out" while the database has units. Cause: Redis drift or holds that never expire because the sweeper is down. Detection: alert when database available minus Redis available exceeds a threshold, and on sweeper lag.

Double charges. Symptom: support tickets about two charges. Cause: retries without idempotency, or an idempotency record written outside the order transaction. Detection: count payments per order id.

What to monitor during the sale

Arrival rate, queue length and admission rate; checkout in-flight count, latency and error rate; lock wait time on the inventory row or Redis latency on the stock key; reservations created, paid, expired per second; Redis-versus-database available difference; payment authorisation latency and decline rate by reason; CDN hit rate; per-customer limit rejections and bot-score distribution. Put them on one screen with a named owner for each degradation switch.
myths: Autoscaling handles flash sales.

Autoscaling reacts in minutes; a flash sale goes from normal to 100× in seconds and is often over before new instances are warm. Worse, the bottleneck is usually one row or one counter for the hot product, which more web servers only hit harder. Flash sales are handled by pre-scaling the stateless tiers and by admission control in front of the stateful ones.
Overselling is prevented by checking stock before decrementing it.

Checking and then decrementing as two steps is exactly what causes overselling: hundreds of requests read 'one left' before any of them writes. The check and the decrement must be one atomic operation — a conditional UPDATE whose row count is the decision, a Redis DECR whose returned value is the decision, or a locked read-modify-write.
Putting inventory in Redis makes it correct.

Redis makes the decrement fast and atomic, but Redis replication is asynchronous: if the primary fails after acknowledging a decrement, the replica may not have it, and units can be sold twice or lost. Redis works as a fast gate in front of a durable source of truth, with reconciliation, not as the only record of what was sold.
A waiting room is only for fairness.

Its first job is capacity protection: it turns an arrival rate the checkout cannot survive into an admission rate it can. Fairness — first come first served versus a randomised draw — is a policy chosen on top. Without admission control the site falls over and nobody, fair or not, gets to buy.
When the units are reserved, the sale is over.

Reservations expire. If 30% of reserving shoppers abandon payment, 30% of the stock comes back to the pool over the next ten minutes, in waves as holds time out. A design that shows 'sold out' permanently at the first zero leaves units unsold; one that keeps everyone waiting forever wastes their time. Show 'sold out, check back' and admit more users as holds expire.
lab:
Goal: reproduce overselling with real concurrent database connections, then remove it with one conditional UPDATE. Python 3.12 standard library (sqlite3, threading), about 10 seconds.

"""Oversell race: 50 units, 200 concurrent buyers. Read-check-write vs atomic decrement."""
import sqlite3, threading, os, tempfile, time

DB = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "shop.db")
STOCK, BUYERS = 50, 200

def reset():
    c = sqlite3.connect(DB); c.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
    c.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS inventory"); c.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS orders")
    c.execute("CREATE TABLE inventory (sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY, available INTEGER)")
    c.execute("CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, buyer INTEGER)")
    c.execute("INSERT INTO inventory VALUES ('PS9', ?)", (STOCK,)); c.commit(); c.close()

def naive(buyer):                      # SELECT, decide in the app, UPDATE: the classic oversell
    c = sqlite3.connect(DB, timeout=30, isolation_level=None)
    (left,) = c.execute("SELECT available FROM inventory WHERE sku='PS9'").fetchone()
    time.sleep(0.001)                  # app logic + network hop between read and write
    if left > 0:
        c.execute("UPDATE inventory SET available = ? WHERE sku='PS9'", (left - 1,))
        c.execute("INSERT INTO orders (buyer) VALUES (?)", (buyer,))
    c.close()

def atomic(buyer):                     # one conditional UPDATE; the row count is the decision
    c = sqlite3.connect(DB, timeout=30, isolation_level=None)
    c.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")
    cur = c.execute("UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 1 "
                    "WHERE sku='PS9' AND available >= 1")
    if cur.rowcount == 1:
        c.execute("INSERT INTO orders (buyer) VALUES (?)", (buyer,))
    c.execute("COMMIT"); c.close()

for fn in (naive, atomic):
    reset(); t0 = time.perf_counter()
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=fn, args=(i,)) for i in range(BUYERS)]
    for t in ts: t.start()
    for t in ts: t.join()
    c = sqlite3.connect(DB)
    sold = c.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders").fetchone()[0]
    left = c.execute("SELECT available FROM inventory").fetchone()[0]
    print(f"{fn.__name__:>6}: orders={sold:>3}  stock left={left:>3}  "
          f"oversold={max(0, sold - STOCK):>3}  ({time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f}s)")
  1. The naive run should report far more orders than 50 — often all 200 — and stock left well above zero: overselling and lost updates at once, because each write overwrote the others' decrements. The atomic run reports exactly 50 orders and 0 left.
  2. Remove the time.sleep. The naive version oversells less but still does: the window between read and write is shorter, not closed.
  3. Try the optimistic variant: read available and a version, then UPDATE … WHERE version = ? and retry on row count 0. Count retries per buyer — under this contention most attempts fail, which is why optimistic locking is wrong for the hottest row.
  4. Shard it: 5 rows of 10 units, each buyer picking a random row and falling back to the others on zero. Count how many buyers were told "sold out" while another row still had stock if you remove the fallback.
recap: A flash sale is a fixed, small amount of inventory meeting a sudden demand many times larger, so most requests must be turned away cheaply and the few that can succeed must be handled exactly once.
Working the spike by hand shows where it breaks: page views can be absorbed by a CDN, but checkout writes and the inventory counter cannot scale with demand.
A waiting room converts the arrival rate into an admission rate the checkout can handle, set by a feedback loop on checkout load and by remaining inventory.

Overselling comes from check-then-act; the fix is an atomic decrement whose result is the decision: a conditional UPDATE with a row-count check, a row lock, a Redis DECR or Lua script, or a sharded counter.
A single hot row serialises every buyer; Redis moves the counter to memory, and sharded counters split it across keys at the cost of false 'sold out' when one shard empties first.
Redis is a fast gate, the database is the source of truth, and the two are reconciled.
A reservation holds a unit for a few minutes; it ends in exactly one of paid, expired or cancelled, enforced by conditional state transitions.
Payments use idempotency keys, authorise at checkout and capture later, and treat a timeout as unknown until confirmed.
Bots are fought with per-account and per-card limits, verification and challenges at the queue, and by making the queue rather than speed decide who buys.
Graceful degradation means switching off everything that is not browsing the product or buying it, and serving 'sold out' from cache.
glossary: Deciding how many users or requests are allowed into a system per unit time, and holding or rejecting the rest.
Asking the card issuer to reserve an amount on the buyer's card without moving money yet.
Turning an earlier authorisation into an actual charge.
A challenge meant to be easy for people and hard for automated scripts, such as identifying images.
Content delivery network: servers near users that cache and serve pages and files so requests do not reach the origin.
Reading a value, deciding, and writing in separate steps, so another actor can change the value in between.
An UPDATE with a WHERE clause that only matches if the precondition holds (such as available ≥ 1), so the database checks and writes atomically.
A loop that measures an output (checkout load) and adjusts an input (admission rate) to hold the output near a target.
Turning off non-essential features under load so the essential path keeps working.
A single database row or cache key receiving so many writes that it, not the fleet, limits throughput.
A client-chosen identifier sent with a request so that retries of the same request have their effect only once.
Two transactions read the same value and both write a result based on it, so one write silently overwrites the other.
Confirming more orders than there are units in stock.
The application servers and databases behind the CDN, where requests that cannot be served from cache end up.
A temporary claim on a unit for one shopper, with an expiry after which the unit returns to stock.
A single logical counter split across several keys or rows, each holding part of the total, to spread write load.
Stock-keeping unit: one distinct sellable item, such as one product in one size and colour; inventory is counted per SKU.
Data plus a cryptographic signature, so the server can trust data stored on the client (such as a queue position) without a database lookup.
A holding page that queues users before a high-demand flow and admits them at a controlled rate.
drill:
Estimate it

A sneaker drop: 6,000 pairs across 12 sizes (500 each), expected 600,000 arrivals in the first 2 minutes, 12 requests per page view of which 9 are static, checkout costs 8 database writes, and the database has 8,000 writes per second of headroom. Size the origin load, the admission rate and how long admissions run if 40% of admitted users buy. Which counter is hottest?

Answer

Arrivals: 600,000 ÷ 120 s = 5,000 per second; requests 5,000 × 12 = 60,000 per second, of which 3 × 5,000 = 15,000 per second reach the origin. Checkout capacity: 8,000 ÷ 8 = 1,000 checkouts per second, so admit about 1,000 per second (minus a safety margin, say 800). Admissions needed: 6,000 ÷ 0.4 = 15,000, so about 15-19 seconds of admissions before stock is fully reserved, then trickle admissions as holds expire. The hottest counters are the popular sizes, not the product: sizes 9-10 might take 15% of demand each, so their 500 units go in a few seconds while size 14 lingers. Each size is a separate row, so the per-row rate is the admission rate times that size's share — about 150 per second, well within a conditional UPDATE's ceiling. Show sold-out per size from cache.

Diagnose it

Ten minutes into a sale, the site shows "sold out" but the reservations table has 1,200 fewer PAID rows than units, and only 50 active holds. Customers on social media are asking why the sale ended early. Redis is used as the stock gate. What happened and what do you do now?

Answer

Redis is too low by roughly 1,150 units. Likely causes: holds expired in the database (returning units to available there) but the expiry path never incremented Redis; or reservation attempts decremented Redis and then failed in the database (duplicate customer, payment declined, timeout) without incrementing back. Either way the gate is stricter than the truth. Now: run the reconciler — set Redis to total − paid − active holds from the database (about 1,150), flip the sale state back to live, and let the waiting room admit about 1,150 ÷ conversion rate more users. Then fix: every path that returns a unit must update both tiers (ideally the reconciler runs every few seconds so drift is bounded automatically), and alert on the difference between Redis and database available.
qa: E
How do you prevent overselling?

Make the stock check and the decrement one atomic operation, and let its result decide. In SQL: UPDATE inventory SET available = available − 1 WHERE sku = ? AND available ≥ 1, and treat a row count of 1 as success and 0 as sold out. In Redis: DECR and treat a negative result as sold out (and increment it back), or a Lua script that checks and decrements together. Never SELECT the stock, compare in the application and then write it back.
E
Why does a flash sale need a waiting room?

Because demand arrives at a rate the checkout cannot process, and the excess turns into timeouts, retries and a collapsed site where nobody buys. A waiting room holds users on a cheap static page and admits them at a rate the checkout can absorb, so the people admitted complete purchases quickly. It also lets the sale be fair by a chosen rule instead of by who retries hardest.
E
What happens to a reservation if the shopper never pays?

It expires after a fixed time (for example 10 minutes) and the unit returns to available stock. Expiry is done by a conditional transition (reserved → expired only if still reserved and past expiry), run lazily when someone needs stock and actively by a sweeper or delay queue, so units come back promptly.
M
Compare SELECT … FOR UPDATE, a conditional UPDATE and Redis DECR for the inventory decrement.

SELECT FOR UPDATE locks the row for the whole transaction, so throughput is one transaction per lock-hold time — a few hundred per second if the transaction does other work. A conditional UPDATE locks the row only for the statement and commit, so it is simpler and faster, perhaps around a thousand per second on one row. Redis DECR is an in-memory operation, so a single key handles tens of thousands per second or more, but it is not durable in the same way and must be reconciled with the database.
Follow-up: When is the row lock still right? — When the decision needs several reads in one transaction (a bundle of SKUs, a per-customer limit) and throughput per row is modest.
M
Walk through the arithmetic of a 100× spike.

Normal: 2,000 requests per second. A million people arrive in the first minute: about 16,700 per second; at 10 requests per page view that is roughly 167,000 per second, about 80-100×. Eight of those 10 requests are static and served by the CDN, leaving about 33,000 per second at the origin. Checkout is the limit: at 10 database writes per checkout and 10,000 writes per second of headroom, the store can complete 1,000 checkouts per second. With 10,000 units and half of admitted users converting, the waiting room should admit about 1,000 per second for roughly 20 seconds.
M
How do sharded counters work and what is their weakness?

Split 10,000 units over 10 keys of 1,000; each request picks a shard (randomly or by user hash) and decrements it, so write load spreads across 10 keys or shards. The weakness is false sold-out: a shard can hit zero while others still have stock, so on a zero the request must try other shards, and near the end the remaining units are scattered. Rebalance by moving units from full shards to empty ones, or fall back to a single counter for the last few percent.
Follow-up: How do you show the total? — Sum the shards for display, accepting that it is approximate while decrements are in flight.
M
Redis says stock is 0 but the database shows 40 units unsold. What happened?

Reservations or decrements were counted in Redis but never completed: shoppers abandoned, payments failed, or Redis decrements were not paired with database orders because a process died in between. Without a release path, Redis drifts below the truth. Fix with expiry that returns units to both stores, and a reconciler that periodically recomputes available = stock − paid − active holds from the database and corrects Redis.
M
How do you make checkout safe to retry?

The client generates an idempotency key per checkout attempt and sends it with every retry; the server stores the key with the result in the same transaction as the order, and a repeat returns the stored result. The payment call to the processor carries its own idempotency key derived from the order. A timeout from the processor is treated as unknown, resolved by querying the processor or waiting for its webhook, never by charging again.
M
How do you stop bots buying the whole stock?

Make speed and volume useless and identities expensive: limit units per account, per payment card, per shipping address and per device; require a verified account created before the sale; challenge suspicious sessions at the waiting room rather than at checkout; issue queue positions in signed tokens tied to the session; and randomise positions for everyone who arrives before the start so bots gain nothing by arriving at 09:59:59.999. For the most valuable drops, a registration-then-lottery replaces the race entirely.
H
Design the waiting room's admission rate.

Admit at the rate checkout can complete, adjusted continuously. Measure checkout in-flight count and latency; a controller raises admissions when there is headroom and lowers them when latency rises, the way Shopify's stateless queue moves its cutoff using a proportional term on how full its checkout throttle is. Cap total admissions by remaining stock plus a margin for expected abandonment, and stop admitting when available plus active holds would be exhausted.

Follow-up: Why not admit a fixed 1,000 per second? — Because checkout capacity varies with payment provider latency and cache warmth; a fixed rate is either too slow when healthy or overloads when degraded.
H
Payment succeeded but the reservation had already expired. What now?

This is a race between two terminal transitions. Prevent it by making 'mark paid' a conditional transition that succeeds only if the reservation is still in reserved state, and by giving the payment step a grace window (expiry sweeps skip holds with a payment in progress). If it still happens — the processor confirmed after expiry and the unit was resold — either allocate from any remaining stock or refund automatically and apologise; never ship a unit you do not have.

Follow-up: Why authorise and capture separately here? — Authorising reserves money without moving it, so a reservation lost to the race can be released by voiding the authorisation, which is cheaper and cleaner than a refund.
H
What do you degrade, and in what order, when the site is overloaded?

Protect, in order: checkout for admitted users, the product page, then everything else. Turn off personalised recommendations, reviews, search suggestions and live inventory counts; serve the product page and 'sold out' state from the CDN with short TTLs; shed browse traffic before checkout traffic; and switch non-critical writes (analytics, wishlists) to a queue processed later. Prepare these as feature flags and rehearse them, because there is no time to build them during the sale.
H
How would you run the same sale in three regions?

Inventory is global but latency wants it local. Allocate stock per region in advance by expected demand (say 50/30/20), decrement locally, and move unsold units between regions as the sale progresses through a coordinator. A single global counter would add a cross-region round trip to every decrement. Keep orders and payments in each region, with a single global reconciliation of units sold against stock after the sale.

sum: Top-100 and 'what is my rank?' for 100 million players, updated live: what a sorted set must do, how a Redis ZSET's skip list with spans answers rank in O(log n), where one key stops scaling, three ways to shard a leaderboard, approximate ranks from score histograms, daily and weekly boards, ties encoded into the score, and anti-cheat.
prereq: in9
Real-time counting: sorted sets serve small leaderboards, hot counters are split, and approximate structures trade exactness for memory.
in3
Redis keeps data in memory, runs commands on one thread per shard, and a key lives entirely on one shard of a cluster.
al10
A heap keeps the best k items in O(log k) per update but cannot tell an arbitrary item its rank.
al9
A linked list gives O(1) splicing once you are at the right node; finding the node is the slow part.
al27
A Fenwick tree keeps prefix sums over an array with O(log n) updates and queries.
sc7
Partitioning by key hash spreads load evenly; partitioning by range keeps neighbours together but risks hot ranges.
sc10
Events can flow through a log such as Kafka to consumers that build derived views, which can be rebuilt by replaying the log.
why:
A mobile game launches a weekly tournament. On Monday morning the leaderboard is a database table with an index on score, and the top-100 screen loads instantly. By Wednesday there are 30 million players, and the profile screen, which shows "You are ranked #14,203,551", takes eight seconds and pins the database at 100% CPU. The query is SELECT COUNT(*) FROM scores WHERE score > :mine. For a player in the middle of the pack, the index has to be walked across fifteen million entries to answer it — and every player opens their profile after every match. The team caches the rank for five minutes, and players complain that their rank does not move after a win. On Saturday the top 10 fills with scores of 2,147,483,647, the largest 32-bit integer, sent by a modified client.

A leaderboard looks like the simplest system in this collection — a list sorted by score — and it hides three hard problems. First, rank is not a lookup: knowing where you stand requires knowing how many players are above you, and ordinary indexes do not keep that count. Second, a single sorted structure does not shard naturally: the top 100 involves everyone, and splitting players across machines splits the order. Third, the most visible part is the most attacked: the top of the board is where prizes and attention are, so it is where cheating concentrates.

In9 used a Redis sorted set for a leaderboard as one part of a real-time counting system. This lesson goes inside it and past its limits. It works out the requirements and arithmetic for a board of 100 million players; the API; why a Redis sorted set answers rank in logarithmic time (a skip list whose links carry counts, worked by hand on six players); where one sorted set stops scaling; three ways to shard a leaderboard and what each costs; approximate ranks from score histograms; daily and weekly boards; ties encoded into the score; and anti-cheat on the write path. The lab builds a skip list with spans, checks its ranks against sorting, and measures the error of histogram ranks.
primer:
The mental model: a marathon with express lanes

Picture the finishing order of a marathon written on a very long scroll, one runner per line, fastest first. Finding the top 100 is easy: read the first 100 lines. But "what place did runner 48,112 finish?" means counting lines from the top until you find them, and inserting a new result in the right place means finding that place first. Now add express lanes: alongside the scroll, a second list mentions only every fourth runner and next to each entry notes "4 runners from the previous entry". A third list mentions every sixteenth runner with "16 runners from the previous". To find runner 48,112's place, you skim the coarsest list, adding up the "runners skipped" notes, drop to the finer list when you would overshoot, and so on down to the scroll. You visit only a few dozen entries and you have their place: the sum of the notes. That is a skip list with spans, and it is exactly how a Redis sorted set answers "what is my rank?".

Updates work the same way: a runner whose time changes is removed from the scroll and re-inserted at the new position, with the notes along the path adjusted by one. Each operation touches a logarithmic number of entries, which for 100 million runners is a few dozen.

The analogy breaks when the scroll no longer fits on one desk. A sorted set lives on one machine and one thread. Split the scroll between two desks by name and neither desk knows a runner's overall place without asking the other; split it by finishing time and runners keep moving between desks as their times change. Most of the design work in a big leaderboard is choosing how to split the scroll — or deciding that most runners only need to know "you finished in the top 34%", which needs no scroll at all.

The four queries, and why each is different

Everything a leaderboard does is one of four operations. Update a score — after every match, possibly many per second at peak. Top k — the first page of the board, identical for every viewer, so cacheable. My rank — different for every viewer, the expensive one. Around me — the players just above and below, which is "my rank" followed by a range read. A design that answers all four in logarithmic time for one board is a sorted set; a design for 100 million players across daily, weekly and all-time boards is about how many of those boards you can afford to keep exact, and where.

One more framing helps in an interview: a leaderboard is a derived view. The facts are score events — "player 7 scored 1,500 in match 88" — and the board is a sorted projection of them. Treating it that way answers the durability question (keep the events and totals durably; the board can be rebuilt) and the anti-cheat question (validate events before they become facts), and it frees you to keep several views of the same facts — all-time, weekly, regional, approximate — each shaped for the query it serves.
body:
0–5Requirements
5–12Estimates
12–18API & data
18–25Architecture
25–48Deep dives
48–56Failures
56–60Close

1 · Requirements

Functional. (1) Record a player's score after each match: either a running total (points accumulated) or a best score (highest single run). (2) Show the global top 100. (3) Show any player's rank and score. (4) Show the 5 players above and below them. (5) Keep all-time, weekly and daily boards, resetting on schedule, with final standings archived for prizes. (6) Show a friends leaderboard. (7) Remove cheaters. Out of scope, said aloud: matchmaking, the game's own scoring rules, prize payment.

Non-functional. Updates visible within about a second. Top-100 and my-rank queries under 50 ms at p99. Exact ranks at least for the top of the board; the product team may accept approximate ranks further down. Durable: losing the leaderboard store must not lose anyone's score. Abuse-resistant.

Clarifying questions. How many players, how many active daily? Total points or best score — they need different update operations? Do ties share a rank or break by time? Must every player see an exact rank, or is "top 12%" acceptable below some point? Per-region boards or one global board? Are there prizes (which raises the stakes for anti-cheat and for exact, archived final standings)?

2 · Back-of-envelope estimates

Assume 100 million registered players on the all-time board, 10 million daily active, each playing 10 matches a day.

Writes. 10M × 10 = 100M score updates per day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,200 per second on average. Peaks — the evening in the largest region, the last hour of a weekly tournament — run perhaps 10× higher: 12,000 per second. Each match updates three boards (all-time, weekly, daily), so the store sees up to 36,000 sorted-set writes per second at peak.

Reads. Every match ends with a results screen showing rank: about as many my-rank queries as matches, 12,000 per second at peak, plus profile and board views — say 30,000 rank queries per second and 20,000 top-100 views per second. Top 100 is identical for everyone, so a 1-second cache turns 20,000 reads into one read per second per board. Rank queries are per player and cannot be shared.

Memory. A Redis sorted set member costs, roughly, a skip list node (score, back pointer, about 1.33 levels of forward pointer plus span on average, and the member string) and a hash table entry — on the order of 100 bytes for a short member id. All-time: 100M × 100 B ≈ 10 GB. Weekly: only players active that week, say 30M → 3 GB. Daily: 10M → 1 GB. Total about 14 GB, with replicas doubling it.

Per-operation cost. A skip list search over n = 100M with p = 1/4 visits on the order of log4(108) ≈ 13 levels, a few nodes per level — dozens of pointer hops, most of them cache misses into a 10 GB structure, so a few microseconds per ZADD or ZREVRANK. One Redis thread doing such commands manages perhaps 100,000-200,000 per second; with 36,000 writes and 30,000 rank reads at peak, the all-time board's single shard is busy but viable, with little headroom and nothing left for growth. That is the number that motivates sharding and approximate ranks later.

Why not SQL? Top 100 with an index on score is cheap. Rank as COUNT(*) WHERE score > x walks every index entry above x: 50 million for a median player. Even at 10 million entries per second per core, that is 5 seconds per query; at 30,000 queries per second it is impossible. The rank query alone rules out a plain index.

3 · The API

POST /internal/scores                          (game servers only, mTLS + signed payload)
  {match_id, player_id, points: 1500, mode: "ranked", ended_at, signature}
  → 202  (accepted into the log; idempotent on match_id + player_id)

GET /boards/{board}/top?limit=100              board ∈ all | weekly | daily | region:eu …
  → [{rank: 1, player_id, name, score}, …]    (CDN/app cache, 1 s)
GET /boards/{board}/players/{player_id}
  → {rank: 14203551, score: 48210, percentile: 85.8, exact: true}
GET /boards/{board}/players/{player_id}/around?n=5
  → [{rank, player_id, score} × 11]
GET /boards/{board}/friends/{player_id}
  → [{rank_among_friends, player_id, score}, …]

Scores come only from game servers, never from clients — the API's first anti-cheat decision. The ingest call is idempotent on (match_id, player_id) so a retried submission cannot count a match twice. The rank response says whether the rank is exact, because below some depth the system may return an estimate (deep dive C).

4 · The data model

Durable (database / log):
  score_events  (match_id, player_id, points, ended_at, board_period, PRIMARY KEY (match_id, player_id))
  players       (player_id PK, total_points, best_score, updated_at, flagged BOOL)
  standings_archive (board, period, rank, player_id, score)   -- written at period close

Redis (views, rebuildable):
  lb:all                 ZSET  member = player_id, score = encoded score
  lb:weekly:2026-W41     ZSET  (EXPIRE at period end + 7 days)
  lb:daily:2026-10-10    ZSET  (EXPIRE at period end + 2 days)
  lb:hist:all            hash or array of bucket counts (approximate rank)

Use short numeric member ids, not names, to keep members small (100M × 30 extra bytes is 3 GB). Store names in a separate cache keyed by id and join them only for the top 100 and the around-me page.

5 · High-level design and the critical path

Write path. A game server finishes a match and posts signed results. The ingest service verifies the signature, applies plausibility checks (deep dive D), and appends a score event to a durable log (or inserts it into score_events, whose primary key makes it idempotent). A board writer consumes events in order and, in one pipelined batch, updates the player's total in the database and applies ZINCRBY (for running totals) or ZADD … GT (for best score: only replace if higher, Redis 6.2+) to each affected board. Score events carry their match id, and the writer records the last applied offset, so a restart replays without double-counting.

Read path. Top 100: ZRANGE lb:all 0 99 REV WITHSCORES, cached for one second. My rank: ZREVRANK lb:all player (with WITHSCORE on Redis 7.2+ to get the score in the same call), served from a replica to keep load off the primary — a replica may be a few milliseconds behind, which nobody can see. Around me: ZRANGE lb:all (r−5) (r+5) REV WITHSCORES after the rank. Friends: ZMSCORE lb:all f1 f2 … f200 (Redis 6.2+) returns all friends' scores in one call; sort them in the application.

6 · Deep dive A: inside a sorted set — the skip list with spans

What the structure must do. Update a member's score, return the top k, return a member's rank, and return a range around a rank — all in about O(log n). A heap (al10) gives the top 1 cheaply but cannot tell an arbitrary member its rank and cannot find a member to update it without an index. A balanced binary search tree keeps order; if each node also stores the size of its subtree, it becomes an order-statistic tree and can compute rank in O(log n) by adding up the sizes of left subtrees it passes. Redis chose a different structure with the same complexity: a skip list whose links carry counts.

Two structures, one set. A large Redis sorted set is a hash table mapping member → score (so ZSCORE is O(1) and an update can find the old score) plus a skip list of nodes ordered by (score, member). Small sets — by default up to 128 members with values up to 64 bytes (zset-max-listpack-entries and zset-max-listpack-value) — use a listpack instead, a compact array scanned linearly, because for tiny sets scanning is faster and uses less memory than pointers. A leaderboard is far past that threshold.

The skip list. Level 0 is an ordinary sorted linked list of every member. Each node also appears on level 1 with probability 1/4, on level 2 with probability 1/16, and so on (Redis uses p = 1/4 and caps nodes at 32 levels). Each level is a sparser sorted list — an express lane. A search starts at the highest level of the head node, moves right while the next node sorts before the target, and drops down a level when it would overshoot. Because each level has about a quarter of the nodes of the one below, the expected number of steps is proportional to log n. Insertion picks a random level for the new node, finds its position with the same search, and splices it in on each of its levels — O(1) work per level once you are there, as in any linked list (al9).

Spans make rank possible. Each forward link in Redis's skip list stores a span: the number of level-0 elements the link jumps over. Searching for a member, add the span of every link you follow; when you arrive, the sum is the member's 1-based position. Worked on six players, ordered by score descending (a leaderboard uses reverse order; the idea is identical):

PositionPlayerScoreLevels
1Ana9802
2Ben9501
3Cai9003
4Dev8701
5Eli8202
6Fay7001

The top level (level 2) has one link from the head to Cai, with span 3 (it jumps over Ana, Ben and Cai). Level 1 links head → Ana (span 1), Ana → Cai (span 2), Cai → Eli (span 2). Level 0 links every node with span 1. Rank of Eli: at level 2, follow head → Cai (Cai sorts before Eli): total 3. Cai has no further link on level 2, drop to level 1: Cai → Eli: total 5. Arrived — Eli is at position 5, rank 4 counting from 0 as ZREVRANK does. Two links followed instead of five. With 100 million members the same walk follows a few dozen links instead of tens of millions.

What an update costs. Changing Eli's score is: look up the old score in the hash table (O(1)); delete Eli's node from the skip list (a search, then unlink on each of Eli's levels, decreasing by one the span of every link on the path that jumped over Eli); insert a new node at the new position (a search, splice, and split the spans of the links it lands under). Redis optimises the case where the new score keeps the node in the same place by updating it in place. All of it is O(log n) expected.

Where it stops. The structure is excellent and has three hard limits for a huge board. It is one key, so Redis Cluster cannot spread it: the whole 10 GB and every command sit on one shard. It is one thread, so every write and rank query for that board is serialised. And large keys make operations around them slow: deleting a huge sorted set synchronously blocks the server (use UNLINK, which frees memory in the background), and a full resynchronisation of a replica copies the whole dataset. Read replicas absorb rank queries; writes still all land on one primary.

7 · Deep dive B: sharding a leaderboard

When one board outgrows one shard — in memory, write rate or rank queries — you split it yourself. Three options, each with a different cost.

By score range. Shard i holds players whose scores fall in a band [bi, bi+1). The top k comes from the highest band alone. A player's rank is (number of players in all higher bands) + (local rank in their band); keep each band's size in a small counter (or call ZCARD on each higher shard) and the global rank is a handful of O(1) reads plus one O(log n). The costs: scores are heavily skewed — most players have low scores — so equal-width bands would put 90% of players in one shard; set band edges by quantiles of the current distribution instead, and re-balance occasionally. And a player whose score crosses an edge must move shards: remove from one, add to the other, which is two operations on two shards, briefly double-counting or missing the player unless the writer handles it (order the operations add-then-remove and de-duplicate on read, or accept a one-moment glitch).

By player hash. Shard = hash(player_id) mod S. Writes spread perfectly evenly and players never move. But order is split across every shard. Top k: ask each of S shards for its top k and merge the S × k results — cheap, and cacheable anyway. Rank: sum over all shards of the number of players with a higher score, which is ZCOUNT shard (score +inf on every shard, each O(log n), in parallel — a scatter-gather for every rank query. With S = 10 and 30,000 rank queries per second, that is 300,000 ZCOUNTs per second across the cluster: workable, but every query's latency is the slowest shard's.

Tiered: exact top, approximate tail. Keep a single exact sorted set only for players above a threshold score that admits roughly the top 1 million — about 100 MB, fast, one shard — and serve everyone else from a histogram (deep dive C). When a player's score crosses the threshold, add them to the exact board; trim the exact board occasionally with ZREMRANGEBYRANK as the threshold rises. This is what most very large games do in practice, because it matches what players can perceive: the top cares about exact positions, the middle cares about progress.
