8 · Deep dive C: approximate ranks

The idea. A player at rank 48 million does not need the exact position; they need to see it move when they improve. Divide the score range into buckets and keep only a count of players per bucket. A player's rank is the number of players in all higher buckets, plus an estimate of how many in their own bucket are above them.

Worked example. Scores run 0 to 1,000,000; use 1,000 buckets of width 1,000. A player with 52,345 points is in bucket 52, covering 52,000-52,999. Suppose the buckets above (53 to 999) hold 41,200,000 players in total and bucket 52 holds 180,000. Assuming players are spread evenly inside the bucket, the fraction above 52,345 is (52,999 − 52,345) ÷ 1,000 ≈ 0.65, so about 117,000 of them. Estimated rank ≈ 41,200,000 + 117,000 = 41,317,000, and the percentile is 1 − 41.3M ÷ 100M ≈ 58.7% — "top 41%". The error is at most the bucket's population (180,000 here) and usually far less; narrower buckets where players are dense shrink it. The lab measures it: with 100,000 players and 1,000 buckets the mean error is about 3 places.

Keeping it current. On each score change, decrement the old bucket and increment the new one — two O(1) updates. Computing "players in all higher buckets" naively sums up to 1,000 counters; a Fenwick tree (al27) over the bucket counts makes both the update and the suffix sum O(log buckets). Bucket edges set by quantiles (so each bucket holds about the same number of players) make the error uniform across the board; recompute edges daily and rebuild the counts.

What players see. Below the exact threshold, show "Top 41%" or a rounded rank ("~41.3M"), and mark it as approximate in the API. Players care that it moves up after a win; with fine buckets it does.

9 · Deep dive D: time windows, ties and anti-cheat

Daily and weekly boards. Keep one key per period — lb:daily:2026-10-10, lb:weekly:2026-W41 — and have the board writer update the all-time, weekly and daily keys for each event in one pipeline (or a MULTI transaction, if they share a hash tag and must change together). Periods are defined in one timezone (usually UTC) and stated in the product, because "daily" means something different in Tokyo and New York. Set an expiry on each key a few days after its period ends, so old boards disappear without a cleanup job. At period close, snapshot the final standings — at least the top N for prizes — to durable storage before the key can expire, and freeze late-arriving events by their match end time so a match finishing at 23:59:58 counts for the right day. A rolling "last 7 days" board is harder: ZUNIONSTORE of seven daily keys is O(N) plus O(M log M) over every member, so compute it periodically (hourly) for display, not on each read.

Ties. Redis orders equal scores by member, byte by byte, which is arbitrary from the player's point of view. Pick a rule. First to reach the score wins: fold time into the score. A Redis score is a 64-bit double, which represents integers exactly up to 253. Use score = points × 232 + (232 − 1 − t), where t is seconds since the season started; the subtraction makes earlier times larger. With points below 221 (about 2.1 million), the total stays below 253. Worked: Ana and Ben both have 1,500 points; Ana reached it at t = 3,600 s, Ben at t = 7,200 s. Ana's score is 1,500 × 4,294,967,296 + 4,294,963,695 = 6,446,745,907,695; Ben's is 6,446,745,904,095. Ana ranks higher, and dividing by 232 recovers 1,500 for display. Ties share a rank (competition ranking, 1-2-2-4): the rank is 1 + the number of strictly higher scores, i.e. ZCOUNT key (score +inf plus one, an O(log n) call, instead of ZREVRANK, which returns a position and would give tied players different numbers.

Anti-cheat on the write path. The first rule is server-authoritative scoring: clients never submit scores. Game servers compute the outcome of each match and sign the result; the ingest service rejects anything unsigned. The second is plausibility checks before a score reaches any board: a maximum number of points per match for the mode, a maximum gain per hour per player, minimum plausible completion times, and rate limits on matches per player (cd12's limiter, keyed by player). The third is review before visibility at the top: an update that would put a player in the top N goes to a review queue — automatic checks such as replaying the match from its recorded inputs, statistical outlier detection on score velocity, account age and device signals — and appears on the public board only when cleared. The top is small, so expensive checks are affordable exactly where cheating pays most. Finally, removal: banning a cheater appends an event to the log that removes them from every board (ZREM on each), sets flagged in the players table so rebuilds exclude them, and can be a shadow ban — the cheater still sees their own score, but the public reads filter it out — so they do not learn what triggered detection.

10 · Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs

Hot board at the end of a tournament. The weekly board's last hour can see ten times normal writes as players push for prizes. Pre-size the shard, move rank reads to replicas, and cache top-100 aggressively.

Losing Redis. The board is a view; rebuild it from the players table or replay the event log from the last snapshot's offset, using absolute totals (ZADD) rather than increments so replays are idempotent. Serve the cached top 100 and hide exact ranks meanwhile.

Double-counted matches. A retried score submission or a consumer restart replays events. Idempotency on (match_id, player_id) at ingest and a tracked log offset in the writer keep totals correct.

Trade-offs to close on. Exact versus approximate rank (where to draw the line); one sorted set versus sharded boards (simplicity versus capacity); score-range versus hash sharding (cheap rank versus even writes); freshness versus load (1-second caches for top k); and fairness rules (tie-breaking, period boundaries) that must be decided as product policy and encoded precisely.
deep:
Why Redis chose a skip list

A balanced tree such as a red-black tree or an order-statistic tree gives the same O(log n) bounds, so the choice is about engineering. Skip lists are simple to implement correctly, which matters for code that must also support range queries by score, by rank and by lexicographic order. Their memory layout is tunable through p: with p = 1/4, a node has 1/(1 − p) ≈ 1.33 levels on average, so each node carries about 1.33 forward pointers and spans — less than the two child pointers plus metadata of a binary tree node. Adding spans to support rank is a small change to insertion and deletion. And walking a range forward or backward is just following level-0 links, with no parent pointers or stack. The price is randomness: performance is expected, not guaranteed, but the probability of a badly unbalanced skip list on millions of nodes is vanishingly small.

Best score versus total score

The two common scoring models need different update operations, and getting it wrong silently corrupts the board. A running total adds each match's points: ZINCRBY, which is not idempotent — replaying an event adds again — so the writer must track which events it has applied. A best score keeps the maximum: ZADD key GT score member (Redis 6.2+) updates only if the new score is higher, and is naturally idempotent because replaying an old score changes nothing. Where possible, make the writer set absolute values from a durable total (ZADD with the total from the database) rather than increments, so that replays and rebuilds converge on the truth.

Percentiles over distributions, not just counts

A histogram with equal-width buckets wastes resolution where few players are and loses it where many are. Two refinements matter at scale. Quantile buckets — edges placed so each bucket holds the same share of players — give every player roughly the same rank error. And because score distributions drift (a new season starts everyone at zero; a balance change shifts scores), recompute edges from a sample periodically and rebuild counts in the background. For boards where players want "percentile among people like me", keep histograms per segment (region, level band) and combine them, since histograms over disjoint populations simply add.

Snapshots and period boundaries need a clock rule

A weekly board's final standings decide prizes, so "final" must be precisely defined. Use the match end time (from the game server, not the time the event reached the writer) to choose the period, close the period at a published instant, accept late events for a grace window (say 10 minutes) to allow for delayed submissions, then freeze: snapshot the top N to durable storage with the log offset, and ignore events for that period afterwards. Without the grace window, players lose matches they finished before the deadline; without the freeze, a delayed event can change prize winners after they were announced.

Friends and group boards scale differently

A friends board looks like a small leaderboard per user, and maintaining one sorted set per user is a trap: a score change for a player with 500 friends becomes 500 writes, a fan-out on write problem (the same trade-off as news feeds, cd3). Since friend lists are bounded and small, compute on read: one ZMSCORE for up to a few hundred friends, a sort in the application, and a short cache. Persistent groups such as clans or guilds, which are viewed often and have up to thousands of members, are worth a sorted set each, updated by the writer, because there each score change updates exactly one group board.

Rank in a relational database, if you must

Sometimes the board has to live in an existing SQL database. Rank there is slow because a B-tree index stores order but not counts. Two workable patterns borrow this lesson's ideas. A bucket table — one row per score bucket with a player count, updated in the same transaction as the player's score — turns rank into a sum over higher buckets (fast with few buckets) plus a COUNT within the player's own bucket over an index on score, which only walks that one bucket. Or a periodic rank snapshot: a batch job computes RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) every few minutes into a table keyed by player, and the API serves that, accepting minutes of staleness. Both are reasonable for boards of a few million players and modest update rates; neither replaces an in-memory structure for a live board at 100 million.

Real-time pushes versus polling

"Real-time" usually means a player sees their new rank right after a match, which a read after the write gives. Pushing live rank changes to everyone viewing the top 100 is a fan-out problem (cd18): the top 100 changes rarely relative to how often it is viewed, so publish a "top 100 changed" event at most once a second and let clients re-fetch from the cache, rather than streaming every update.
prod:
The reference implementation: Redis's own documentation and source

The Redis documentation presents leaderboards as the canonical use of sorted sets, and its implementation note states the structure precisely: sorted sets are implemented via a dual-ported data structure containing both a skip list and a hash table, so every addition is O(log n), and reading members in order is cheap because they are already sorted. The source (t_zset.c, with constants in server.h) shows the details this lesson relies on: p = 1/4, at most 32 levels, a span stored with every forward link and used to compute rank, and the listpack encoding for sets of up to 128 entries by default. The ZADD page documents the property behind the tie-breaking trick: scores are doubles that represent integers exactly between −253 and +253, and members with equal scores are ordered by binary comparison of their bytes.

Two production details follow from the docs and source. First, version matters: ZADD … GT/LT and ZMSCORE arrived in Redis 6.2, and ZRANK … WITHSCORE in 7.2; a managed service pinned to an older version silently lacks them. Second, the commands that walk ranges or unions — ZRANGE with large windows, ZUNIONSTORE, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE over millions of members — are O(n) in what they touch and block the single thread while they run; schedule them away from peaks or break them into chunks.

Failure modes you will see

Latency spikes on the board shard. Symptom: rank queries jump from 1 ms to 100 ms periodically. Cause: an O(n) command on the big key (a daily union, a large range read, a synchronous DEL of last week's board) blocking the thread. Detection: Redis SLOWLOG and latency monitoring. Fix: UNLINK instead of DEL, chunked range work, move unions off-peak.

Ranks that disagree between screens. Symptom: the results screen says #1,204 and the profile says #1,207. Cause: one reads the primary and one a lagging replica, or one is a cached value. Usually harmless; make it consistent by reading rank and around-me from the same replica in one pipeline.

Impossible scores at the top. Symptom: the top 10 shows maximum-integer scores. Cause: a client-reported score path or a missing plausibility check on a new game mode. Detection: alert on any score above the mode's theoretical maximum. Fix: remove via the log, add the check, review the top-N queue.

Weekly board missing on Monday. Symptom: the new week's board is empty and last week's expired before the prize snapshot. Cause: TTL shorter than the snapshot job's schedule, or the snapshot job failed. Fix: snapshot is a gated step with an alert; TTL is period end plus days, not hours.

What to monitor

Write rate per board and writer lag behind the event log; rank query latency at p99 per shard; Redis memory per board key and its growth; replica lag; slow log entries on board keys; histogram bucket populations (for rank error); plausibility-check rejection rates per game mode; top-N review queue length and age; and the count of players removed for cheating per day.
myths: A leaderboard is a SELECT … ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 100.

That works for the top 100 with an index on score. 'What is my rank?' is the hard query: in SQL it is COUNT(*) WHERE score > mine, which on a B-tree index scans every entry above you — 50 million rows for a median player. Ordinary indexes do not store subtree counts, so rank is linear. A structure that keeps counts (a skip list with spans, an order-statistic tree) makes it logarithmic.
Redis sorted sets scale to any size because Redis Cluster shards data.

Cluster shards keys, not the inside of a key. One leaderboard is one key, so all of its members, memory and commands live on one shard and one thread. At 100 million members that is around 10 GB on one node, with every update and rank query serialised on it. Beyond that you shard the leaderboard yourself.
Ties are handled automatically.

Redis orders equal scores by member name, byte by byte — so 'player_a' beats 'player_z' at the same score, which is rarely the rule you want. If 'who got there first' should win, encode it into the score; if tied players should share a rank, compute rank as 1 + the number of strictly higher scores, not as a position.
Exact rank matters for everyone.

A player at rank 48,203,117 cannot tell it apart from 48,203,450, and the number changes many times a second anyway. Exact ranks matter near the top; for everyone else a percentile ('top 34%') or a rank computed from a score histogram is both cheaper and more honest. Choosing where exactness stops is a product decision that removes most of the scaling problem.
Anti-cheat is a separate system that can come later.

If the client reports its own score, the leaderboard is a list of whoever edited a request first, and the top 100 — the only part most people look at — fills with impossible scores within hours. Scores must be computed or validated by the server before they reach the board, which is a design decision for the write path, not an add-on.
lab:
Goal: build a skip list with spans, check that it answers rank exactly like sorting does, and measure how far a 1,000-bucket histogram's rank estimate is off. Python 3.12 standard library, a few seconds.

"""Skip list with spans (how a ZSET computes rank), checked against sorting, plus histogram ranks."""
import bisect, random, time

P, MAX_LEVEL = 0.25, 32                     # Redis: p = 1/4, at most 32 levels

class Node:
    __slots__ = ("key", "fwd", "span")
    def __init__(self, key, level):
        self.key, self.fwd, self.span = key, [None] * level, [0] * level

class SkipList:                              # keys are (-score, member): rank 0 = highest score
    def __init__(self):
        self.head, self.level, self.n = Node(None, MAX_LEVEL), 1, 0

    def insert(self, key):
        update, rank, x = [None] * MAX_LEVEL, [0] * MAX_LEVEL, self.head
        for i in range(self.level - 1, -1, -1):          # walk down, counting skipped nodes
            rank[i] = 0 if i == self.level - 1 else rank[i + 1]
            while x.fwd[i] and x.fwd[i].key < key:
                rank[i] += x.span[i]; x = x.fwd[i]
            update[i] = x
        lv = 1
        while random.random() < P and lv < MAX_LEVEL: lv += 1
        if lv > self.level:
            for i in range(self.level, lv):
                rank[i], update[i] = 0, self.head; self.head.span[i] = self.n
            self.level = lv
        node = Node(key, lv)
        for i in range(lv):                              # splice in and split the spans
            node.fwd[i] = update[i].fwd[i]; update[i].fwd[i] = node
            node.span[i] = update[i].span[i] - (rank[0] - rank[i])
            update[i].span[i] = rank[0] - rank[i] + 1
        for i in range(lv, self.level): update[i].span[i] += 1
        self.n += 1

    def rank(self, key):                                 # 0-based: sum the spans you jump over
        r, x = 0, self.head
        for i in range(self.level - 1, -1, -1):
            while x.fwd[i] and x.fwd[i].key <= key:
                r += x.span[i]; x = x.fwd[i]
            if x.key == key: return r - 1
        return None

random.seed(7); N = 100_000
players = {f"p{i}": random.randint(0, 1_000_000) for i in range(N)}
sl, t = SkipList(), time.perf_counter()
for m, s in players.items(): sl.insert((-s, m))
print(f"inserted {N:,} in {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s; levels used: {sl.level}")
exact = sorted((-s, m) for m, s in players.items())
for m in random.sample(list(players), 1000):
    assert sl.rank((-players[m], m)) == bisect.bisect_left(exact, (-players[m], m))
print("1,000 rank queries match the sorted list")

BUCKET = 1_000                                           # approximate rank from a histogram
hist = [0] * (1_000_000 // BUCKET + 1)
for s in players.values(): hist[s // BUCKET] += 1
suffix = [0] * (len(hist) + 1)
for b in range(len(hist) - 1, -1, -1): suffix[b] = suffix[b + 1] + hist[b]
errs = []
for m in random.sample(list(players), 1000):
    s = players[m]; b = s // BUCKET
    approx = suffix[b + 1] + hist[b] * (1 - (s - b * BUCKET + 0.5) / BUCKET)
    errs.append(abs(approx - sl.rank((-s, m))))
print(f"approx rank error: mean {sum(errs)/len(errs):.1f}, max {max(errs):.1f} of {N:,} players")
  1. Expect about 9 levels for 100,000 members (log4 100,000 ≈ 8.3), all 1,000 rank checks passing, and a histogram error of a few places on average.
  2. Count the links followed in rank() and print the average: it should be a few dozen, against an average position of 50,000.
  3. Change the scores to a skewed distribution (int(random.paretovariate(1.5) * 1000)) and rerun the histogram: the error grows in the crowded low buckets. Then use quantile edges (sort a sample, take every 100th value as an edge) and watch it fall.
recap: A leaderboard must update scores, return the top k, return any player's rank and the players around them, all in real time.
A heap gives top k but not rank; a database index gives order but rank needs a count of everything above you.
A Redis sorted set pairs a hash table (member to score) with a skip list ordered by score whose links store spans, so rank is the sum of spans walked: O(log n).
One sorted set lives on one shard: at 100 million members it is about 10 GB and one thread, so very large boards are sharded by score range or by player hash.
Range sharding answers rank as the count of players in higher shards plus a local rank; hash sharding spreads writes evenly but needs a scatter-gather for rank and a merge for top k.
Approximate ranks come from a histogram of score buckets: players in higher buckets plus an interpolation inside your bucket.
Daily and weekly boards are separate keys written alongside the all-time board, expired after the period, and archived at period end.
Ties are a rule: encode the tie-breaker into the score within 53 bits, or compute competition rank as 1 + count of strictly higher scores.
The source of truth is a durable log or database of score events; Redis boards are rebuildable views.
Anti-cheat means server-authoritative scores, plausibility limits on the write path, review before the top ranks, and the ability to remove a player from every board.
glossary: A ranking where tied scores share a rank and the next rank skips ahead (1, 2, 2, 4), computed as 1 plus the number of strictly higher scores.
A ranking where tied scores share a rank and the next rank does not skip (1, 2, 2, 3).
Combining results from many shards into one answer, as in merging each shard's top k.
Counts of how many players have scores in each fixed range, used to estimate rank without storing order.
Redis's compact encoding for small collections: a single contiguous block scanned linearly, used for sorted sets of up to 128 entries by default.
A balanced search tree whose nodes store subtree sizes, so it can find an element's rank or the k-th element in O(log n).
The percentage of players with a lower score; 'top 5%' is the 95th percentile.
Sending one query to every shard in parallel and combining the replies.
A design where the server computes or validates the game outcome instead of trusting what the client reports.
Hiding a suspected cheater's scores from everyone else while they still see their own, so they do not learn they were detected.
A sorted linked list with extra randomly chosen express lanes of forward links, giving expected O(log n) search, insert and delete.
A Redis data type holding unique members each with a numeric score, kept ordered by score.
In a Redis skip list, the number of elements a forward link jumps over; summing spans along a search gives rank.
drill:
Design it

A puzzle game has 40 million players. The product wants: a global all-time board, a weekly board with prizes for the top 1,000, exact ranks for the top 100,000, and "Top X%" for everyone else. Peak is 20,000 score updates per second. Ties go to whoever reached the score first. Sketch the data structures, the update path and the memory.

Answer

All-time: an exact sorted set holding only players above the score of rank ~120,000 (a margin over 100,000), about 12 MB, plus a histogram of all 40M players over 2,000 quantile buckets for percentiles. Weekly: an exact sorted set of everyone active that week (say 15M × 100 B ≈ 1.5 GB) because prizes need exact final standings for the top 1,000; key per week with expiry two weeks after, and a gated snapshot of the top 1,000 at close. Scores encoded as points × 232 + (232 − 1 − seconds since season start), so points must stay under ~2.1 million. Update path: signed result → ingest checks → event log → writer pipelines ZADD/ZINCRBY on the weekly board, the histogram move (old bucket −1, new +1), and the exact all-time board if the new score clears its threshold. 20,000 updates per second spread over these keys is comfortable for two or three shards. Top 1,000 weekly entries pass through a review queue before prizes.

Diagnose it

After moving the all-time board to a hash-sharded design with 16 shards, p99 latency for "my rank" rose from 2 ms to 40 ms, while p50 barely changed. Writes are fine. Why, and what are your options?

Answer

Rank on a hash-sharded board is a scatter-gather: ZCOUNT on all 16 shards, and the query waits for the slowest. Tail latency of a fan-out is roughly the tail of the worst of 16 calls, so occasional slowness on any shard (a slow command, a garbage-collection pause in the proxy, a network blip) now hits most queries' p99 — while the median is unaffected. Options: send rank queries to replicas and use hedged requests (resend to another replica if one is slow); cache each player's rank briefly after a write; move to score-range sharding, where rank is a few cached band counts plus one local ZREVRANK; or switch to exact-top-plus-histogram, which makes rank a single small sorted set or an O(log buckets) histogram query.
qa: E
How would you build a game leaderboard?

A Redis sorted set per board: member = player id, score = points. ZADD or ZINCRBY updates a score in O(log n); ZREVRANGE (or ZRANGE … REV) 0 99 returns the top 100; ZREVRANK returns a player's rank in O(log n); ZREVRANGE around that rank returns their neighbours. Persist score events durably elsewhere so the board can be rebuilt.
E
Why is 'my rank' harder than 'top 100'?

Top 100 reads the first 100 entries of an ordered structure. Rank requires knowing how many entries are above you; a normal ordered index does not store counts, so it must walk them all. Structures that store counts per link or subtree, such as a skip list with spans or an order-statistic tree, answer rank in O(log n).
E
How does Redis store a sorted set?

Small sets (by default up to 128 members with short values) use a listpack, a compact array scanned linearly. Larger ones use two structures together: a hash table from member to score for O(1) score lookups, and a skip list ordered by (score, member) whose forward links store spans for rank. Updates touch both.
M
Explain how a skip list answers rank in O(log n).

Each node has a random number of levels, with each level holding a forward link and a span: how many elements that link jumps over. To find a member's rank, start at the top level of the head, move forward while the next node sorts before or at the target, adding each link's span, and drop a level when you cannot move. The sum of spans when you reach the node is its 1-based rank. Expected path length is O(log n) because each level has about a quarter of the nodes of the one below (Redis uses p = 1/4).
Follow-up: Why a skip list and not a balanced tree? — Simpler to implement and to extend with spans and range walks, with the same expected complexity; Redis's author chose it for that simplicity.
M
How much memory does a 100-million-player leaderboard need in Redis?

Roughly 100 bytes per member for the skip list node, the hash table entry and a short member string — about 10 GB. It fits one large node, but a snapshot fork may need copy-on-write headroom, failover must reload or resync 10 GB, and every update and query runs on that shard's one thread. Measure with MEMORY USAGE on a sample before deciding.
Follow-up: How do you shrink it? — Use short numeric member ids, keep only active players in the live board, and serve inactive players from a percentile estimate.
M
Compare sharding a leaderboard by score range and by player hash.

Range shards each own a band of scores; top k comes from the top shard alone, and rank is the count of players in all higher shards plus the local rank — cheap if per-shard counts are kept. But scores are skewed, so bands must be set by quantiles, and a player crossing a band boundary must move shards. Hash shards spread writes evenly and never move players, but top k needs the top k of every shard merged, and rank needs ZCOUNT of higher scores on every shard — a scatter-gather per query.
M
How do you implement daily and weekly boards?

Separate keys per period, such as lb:daily:2026-10-10 and lb:weekly:2026-W41, updated in the same pipeline as the all-time board when a score event arrives. Give each an expiry a little after the period ends, and archive the final standings to durable storage at period close so prizes and history do not depend on Redis. Avoid computing weekly boards by unioning dailies on read; it is O(n) over every member.
M
Two players have the same score. Who ranks higher?

It is a product rule, and Redis's default — order by member bytes — is almost never it. For 'first to reach the score wins', encode time into the score: score = points × 2^32 + (2^32 − 1 − seconds since season start), which fits in the 53 bits a double holds exactly if points stay below about 2 million. For 'ties share a rank', compute rank as 1 + ZCOUNT of scores strictly greater than the player's.
Follow-up: What breaks if you exceed 2^53? — Scores lose precision, so two different encoded values may become equal and the tie-breaker silently stops working.
M
How would you show a friends leaderboard?

Friend lists are small, so compute it on read: fetch the friends' scores with one ZMSCORE call on the all-time board (Redis 6.2+), sort in the application, and cache briefly. Maintaining a separate sorted set per user would multiply writes by the number of followers for every score change.
H
Design approximate ranks for 100 million players.

Keep exact rank only where it matters, say the top 10,000 in a capped sorted set. For everyone else, maintain a histogram: counts of players per score bucket (for example 1,000 buckets), updated by moving a player from the old bucket to the new one on each score change. Rank ≈ players in all higher buckets + an interpolation within the player's bucket. Keep prefix sums in a Fenwick tree so each update and query is O(log buckets). The error is bounded by the population of one bucket, so make buckets narrower where players are dense.
Follow-up: How do you choose bucket edges? — By quantiles of the current distribution, recomputed occasionally, so each bucket holds a similar number of players and the error is uniform.
H
How do you keep the top of the board free of cheaters?

Make scores server-authoritative: game servers compute match results and sign them; the leaderboard writer accepts only signed results. Apply plausibility checks on the write path (maximum points per match, maximum gain per hour, impossible completion times). Hold entries that would enter the top N for automatic or human review before they become visible. Remove confirmed cheaters from every board via the event log so rebuilds do not reintroduce them, and consider shadow banning so they do not learn what triggered detection.
Follow-up: Why review only the top? — It is where cheating pays (prizes, visibility) and where users look, and it is small enough for expensive checks such as replay verification.
H
Redis lost the leaderboard. How do you recover?

Redis is a derived view. Rebuild it from the durable source of truth: either the players table of current totals (stream it into ZADD in batches of a few thousand with pipelining), or the score event log replayed from the last snapshot. Meanwhile serve the last cached top 100 and hide 'my rank' or show the last known value. For a 100-million board, rebuilding at a few hundred thousand ZADDs per second takes minutes, which is why a replica and periodic RDB snapshots exist to make a full rebuild rare.

Follow-up: How do you avoid missing events that arrive during the rebuild? — Record the log offset at which the snapshot was taken, rebuild from the snapshot, then replay the log from that offset with idempotent ZADDs (setting absolute totals rather than increments).

t: Design live comments and reactions for a streaming event (Twitch chat, YouTube Live)
sum: Five million viewers on one stream: holding the connections, a fan-out tree that sends each message once per server instead of once per viewer, sampling and rate limits when chat is faster than anyone can read, reactions aggregated into counts, moderation in the path, per-stream ordering, and the hot-stream and reconnect-storm problems — with Twitch's Edge/Pubsub design and LinkedIn's live-likes system as the real cases.
prereq: cd2
Chat: persistent connections on connection servers, a registry of which server holds which user, and fan-out to groups.
net11
WebSockets give a full-duplex connection; Server-Sent Events stream server-to-client over plain HTTP; both keep one long-lived connection per client.
cd12
A rate limiter keeps a token bucket per key and rejects or delays requests beyond the configured rate.
sc10
Pub/sub decouples publishers from subscribers through topics; delivery can be at-most-once or at-least-once.
in1
A durable log such as Kafka retains messages by offset so consumers can replay, at the cost of each consumer reading whole partitions.
net13
A server holds many sockets with event-driven I/O (epoll); each connection costs kernel buffers and file descriptors.
sc12
Retries with exponential backoff and jitter keep many clients from retrying in lockstep.
why:
The final of an esports tournament is streaming to five million people. The chat panel beside the video is part of the event: viewers cheer, spam an emote when a player makes a play, ask questions the casters read out. In the deciding moment, a tenth of the audience types at once. A naive chat backend takes each new message and sends it to every connected viewer. At 8,000 messages per second and 5 million viewers, that is 40 billion deliveries per second; the chat servers saturate their network links within seconds, messages arrive a minute late, then not at all, and the connection servers start dropping viewers, who all reconnect at the same moment and knock over the servers that were still standing. Meanwhile, someone posts a slur that is shown to everyone before anyone can remove it, and a bot posts the same scam link four hundred times.

Live comments look like group chat (cd2) with a bigger group, but the numbers change the problem. In a group chat of 100, everyone should receive every message, durably, in order. In a live chat of five million, nobody can read more than a handful of messages per second, so delivering everything is not just expensive but pointless; the audience joins and leaves in waves around the broadcast; reactions arrive at a million per second; and anything harmful is shown to millions within a second unless it is stopped before fan-out. The design is about fan-out economics and deliberate loss.

This lesson works through the design in interview order: requirements; the arithmetic of connections, message rates, deliveries and bandwidth; the API and data model; the architecture and the path of one message; then three deep dives. The first is the fan-out topology: subscription registries, trees of relays, encoding once and batching. The second is what to do when chat is too fast to read: rate limits, slow mode, per-viewer sampling with a directed lane for messages that matter, and reaction aggregation. The third is moderation in the path, ordering, and the hot-stream and reconnect-storm failures. The real cases are Twitch's description of its Edge and Pubsub chat tiers and LinkedIn's system that streams a million likes per second; the lab measures how much sampling, batching and aggregation remove.
primer:
The mental model: a stadium, a PA system and a scoreboard

Picture a stadium of 80,000 people. Everyone can shout, but nobody hears every voice; you hear the people near you and the roar of the crowd. The stadium does not try to relay every shout to every seat. Instead it has a public-address system that carries a few selected voices (the announcer reading out messages) over the public-address (PA) system to every section through a hierarchy of amplifiers — one feed to each section's speakers, not one to each seat. It has a big screen that shows the crowd's mood as one number ("noise level: 112 dB") rather than each scream. Stewards stop people with banners that break the rules before they reach the front, not after the cameras have shown them. And the gates control how fast people enter, because 80,000 people pushing through at once crush each other.

Each piece maps onto the design. The sections and their speakers are edge servers, each holding the connections of tens of thousands of viewers. The amplifier hierarchy is the fan-out tree: a message is sent once to each edge, which delivers it locally. The announcer's selection is sampling: each viewer sees a readable subset of the chat. The screen's noise level is reaction aggregation: counts, not events. The stewards are moderation in the path. The gates are admission and reconnect control.

The analogy breaks in one place that matters: in a stadium everyone hears the same PA. Online, each viewer can get a slightly different sample, plus messages meant only for them — replies, mentions, their own message appearing instantly. So the design has two delivery lanes: a broadcast lane that is the same for everyone on the stream, and a directed lane for messages addressed to one viewer.

Two paths with opposite needs

The write path handles each accepted message once: authenticate the sender, apply their rate limit and the channel's rules, run moderation, assign a sequence number, publish. It must be strict and consistent but its volume is modest — thousands per second even for a huge stream. The read path multiplies each message by the audience: it must be cheap per delivery, tolerant of loss, and scale with the number of viewers. Every design decision below belongs to one of the two paths, and confusing them — durable, ordered, acknowledged delivery on the read path; best-effort checks on the write path — is where weak designs go wrong.

A useful sentence to say early in the interview: the write path is a per-stream sequencer with rules; the read path is a cache-like broadcast that is allowed to drop. It tells the interviewer you know where correctness lives (accepting, rejecting and ordering messages, which happens once per message) and where scale lives (delivering, which happens millions of times per message), and it sets up every later trade-off — sampling, batching, at-most-once delivery — as a deliberate choice on the read path rather than a corner cut.

1 · Requirements

Functional. (1) Viewers of a live stream see a chat panel that updates in real time. (2) Signed-in viewers can post messages; their own message appears instantly. (3) Viewers can send reactions (hearts, emotes) shown as a live aggregate. (4) Moderators and the streamer can delete messages, time out or ban users, enable slow mode, restrict chat to followers or subscribers. (5) Replies and mentions reach the person addressed. (6) Chat is saved and can be replayed in sync with the recording. Out of scope, said aloud: the video pipeline itself (cd4), private messages, and payment for paid messages (beyond treating them as must-deliver).

Non-functional. Low latency: a message should appear for viewers within about a second of being sent, roughly in step with the video (which itself runs several seconds behind real time). Massive fan-out: support single streams with millions of concurrent viewers and many thousands of streams at once. Availability over completeness: losing an occasional message on the read path is acceptable; the chat going dark is not. Safety: harmful content must be stopped before broad delivery wherever possible. Consistent order within a stream.

Clarifying questions. What is the largest single stream (viewers, chatters)? How many concurrent streams? Must every viewer see every message (a small Q&A) or is sampling acceptable (a big event)? Are there paid or pinned messages that must never be dropped? How fast must moderation act, and is a short chat delay acceptable to the product? Global audience or one region?

2 · Back-of-envelope estimates

Assume the largest event has 5 million concurrent viewers; across the platform there are 20 million concurrent viewers at peak; on the big stream 5% of viewers chat, each sending one message every 30 seconds; a message is about 150 bytes on the wire; each viewer taps a reaction every 5 seconds.

Connections. 20 million concurrent connections platform-wide. LinkedIn reported holding on the order of 100,000 connections per frontend machine in its live-likes system; using that figure, the platform needs about 200 edge servers, plus 50% headroom for failures and spikes: 300. The big stream alone spans 50 edges' worth of viewers, spread across many more edges because viewers of different streams share edges. Memory per idle connection (kernel socket buffers, a goroutine or actor, a little user state) is tens of kilobytes: 100,000 × 20 KB = 2 GB per edge, comfortable.

Message rate. Chatters: 5% × 5,000,000 = 250,000; each sends 1 per 30 s: 250,000 ÷ 30 ≈ 8,300 messages per second into one stream — far beyond readability, which is around 5-10 per second for a human.

Naive fan-out. 8,300 messages × 5,000,000 viewers ≈ 41.5 billion deliveries per second. At 150 bytes each that is about 6 TB/s. Impossible, and pointless.

Sampled fan-out. Cap what a viewer receives at 10 messages per second: 5,000,000 × 10 = 50 million deliveries per second for the stream. Bandwidth: 10 × 150 B = 1.5 KB/s per viewer; × 5 million = 7.5 GB/s (60 Gbit/s) total, before compression. Per edge holding 100,000 of these viewers: 1 million deliveries and about 150 MB/s (1.2 Gbit/s). Batching the messages into one frame every 200 ms turns 10 writes per second per connection into 5: 500,000 socket writes per second per edge. That is the per-edge budget to design for.

Reactions. 5,000,000 viewers ÷ 5 s = 1,000,000 reactions per second inbound. If edges count locally and send a summary every 250 ms, upstream traffic is (edges serving the stream) × 4 per second — a few hundred small messages per second. Outbound, one total every 500 ms per viewer: 10 million tiny updates per second, which ride in the same frames as chat.

Storage. Accepted messages for replay: 8,300 per second × 150 B ≈ 1.25 MB/s for the big stream; a three-hour event is about 13 GB. Platform-wide, perhaps 50,000 messages per second ≈ 650 GB per day. Easy for a partitioned log or wide-column store, written off the hot path.

3 · The API

Connection (WebSocket, or SSE + HTTP POST):
  GET wss://chat.example.com/v1/streams/{stream_id}?resume_from_seq=48211930
  ← server frames, batched every ~200 ms:
     {type: "batch", msgs: [{seq: 48211931, id, user: {id, name, badges}, text, ts}, …],
      reactions: {"❤": 18422, "🔥": 9310}, viewers: 4920331}
     {type: "delete", seq: 48211901}          {type: "mode", slow_mode_s: 10}
  → client frames:
     {type: "send", client_msg_id: "c-7f2…", text: "what a play"}
     {type: "react", emote: "🔥"}

Server replies to send:
  {type: "ack", client_msg_id: "c-7f2…", seq: 48211977}
  | {type: "rejected", client_msg_id, reason: "SLOW_MODE", retry_after_s: 7}

Moderation (HTTP, moderators only):
  POST /v1/streams/{id}/messages/{msg_id}:delete
  POST /v1/streams/{id}/users/{user_id}:timeout   {seconds: 600}
  PATCH /v1/streams/{id}/settings                  {slow_mode_s: 10, followers_only: true}

The client_msg_id lets the client show its own message instantly and match the server's ack, and makes a resend after a dropped connection idempotent. resume_from_seq lets a reconnecting client pick up from the last message it displayed. Rejections carry a reason and a retry hint so the client can show "slow mode: wait 7 s" instead of letting the user mash send.

4 · The data model

In memory, on the stream's ingest/stream node:
  stream_state  {stream_id, next_seq, slow_mode_s, followers_only, blocklist_version}
  recent_ring   last ~1,000 broadcast messages (for resume and new joiners)
  user_limits   token bucket per (stream, user)  — or in a shared store (cd12)

In memory, on each edge:
  subscriptions  stream_id → set of local connections
  conn_state     connection → {user_id, stream_id, last_seq_sent}

Shared, small, fast (replicated cache):
  bans / timeouts   (stream_id, user_id) → until
  registry          stream_id → set of edges with viewers   (for routing)
  user_location     user_id → edge                          (for the directed lane)

Durable, off the hot path:
  chat_log   PARTITION BY (stream_id, hour) CLUSTER BY seq:
             {seq, msg_id, user_id, text, ts, deleted_at, moderation_flags}

Almost everything on the read path is in memory and reconstructible: if an edge dies, its subscriptions die with its connections, and the clients re-create them by reconnecting. The only durable data is the chat log (for replay and moderation review) and moderation state (bans must survive restarts).

5 · High-level design and the path of one message

  1. Send. The viewer's client shows the message immediately (greyed until acknowledged) and sends it on its connection to its edge.
  2. Ingest. The edge forwards it to the stream's ingest node — one node (or partition) owns each stream's write path, chosen by hashing the stream id. The node checks the sender's ban and timeout state, the per-user token bucket and slow mode, the channel's mode (followers only), and runs fast moderation filters. It assigns the next sequence number and acks the sender.
  3. Publish. The stream node puts the message into the broadcast lane (subject to sampling, deep dive B) and, if it mentions or replies to someone, into the directed lane for those users. It appends it asynchronously to the chat log.
  4. Fan out. The broadcast lane goes through relays to every edge in the stream's registry; directed messages go straight to the edge holding each addressed user.
  5. Deliver. Each edge collects messages for 200 ms, builds one frame per stream (encoding it once), and writes the same bytes to every subscribed local connection, adding the few directed messages per connection.

Viewer joins follow the reverse path: the client connects to an edge (any edge — the load balancer chooses), the edge adds the connection to its local subscription set and, if it is the edge's first viewer of the stream, registers itself in the stream's registry so messages start flowing to it; it then sends the last few dozen messages from the recent ring so the panel is not empty.

6 · Deep dive A: the fan-out topology

Option 1: every edge receives everything. The simplest pub/sub broadcasts every message of every stream to every edge, and each edge drops what it has no viewers for. With 300 edges and 50,000 messages per second platform-wide, each edge processes 50,000 messages per second mostly to discard them, and the publisher sends 15 million per second. It wastes work proportional to edges × streams, and does not scale.

Option 2: route by subscription. Keep a registry of which edges have viewers for which stream. A message for stream S goes only to edges in S's registry entry. LinkedIn's live-likes system describes this shape: each frontend node keeps an in-memory table of which of its connections watch which video; it tells a dispatcher tier which videos it has viewers for; the subscription table lives in a key-value store any dispatcher can read; on publish, a dispatcher looks up the frontends interested in that video and sends only to them, and each frontend routes to its local connections. Twitch's chat describes a similar split between an Edge tier holding connections and a Pubsub tier that distributes messages across Edge nodes, which together "form a hierarchical message distribution system". The publisher's cost is now proportional to the number of edges that actually serve the stream.

Option 3: a tree for the biggest streams. A stream with viewers on 100 edges means 100 sends per message from one node. At 200 messages per second in the broadcast lane that is 20,000 sends per second — fine. But at the raw 8,300 per second it would be 830,000, and the stream node also does ingest. Insert relays: the stream node sends to 10 relays, each relay to 10 edges. Each node's fan-out is bounded (10), the tree's depth is log10(edges), and adding a level costs one more network hop — a millisecond or two. Discord's Manifold applies the same idea inside a cluster: group recipients by the node they live on and send one message per node, which then fans out locally.

Encode once, write many. At the edge, the expensive part is the per-connection write. Serialise each 200 ms batch for a stream once into its wire bytes (and compress once, if using compression), then write those same bytes to every connection subscribed to the stream. Per-connection work becomes a system call with a shared buffer, not JSON encoding. Directed messages are the exception, appended per connection. This is the difference between an edge that serves 100,000 viewers and one that serves 10,000.

Batching as a dial. A 200 ms batch window cuts socket writes from 10 to 5 per second per viewer at 10 messages per second, and to 5 regardless of how fast chat runs. Longer windows save more and add delay; at 500 ms the chat feels sluggish. 100-250 ms is the usual range, and it can adapt: send immediately when chat is quiet, batch when it is busy.

7 · Deep dive B: when chat is too fast to read

Control what enters. Three limits apply on ingest. A per-user token bucket (cd12) — say one message per second with a burst of three — stops individuals flooding. Slow mode, set by the streamer, raises that to one message per N seconds for everyone. And a per-stream ingest cap bounds the worst case for one stream: beyond, say, 2,000 accepted messages per second, further messages are accepted for the sender (they see their own message) and the log, but are not eligible for the broadcast lane. Duplicate detection — the same text from one user within a short window, or the same link from many new accounts — rejects copy-paste spam before it costs anything downstream.

Sample what each viewer sees. Even after limits, a big stream's chat outruns readers. The stream node therefore builds a broadcast lane capped at a readable rate — say 10-20 messages per second — chosen from accepted messages. Random sampling is fair and simple; weighted sampling can favour subscribers, longer or non-duplicate messages, or messages a ranking model scores as higher quality, but keep a random component so no group dominates. Because the sample is chosen once at the stream node and fanned out, every viewer of the stream sees the same broadcast messages, which keeps conversations coherent ("did you see what X said?").

Never sample away what matters. A directed lane carries messages that must reach a specific viewer regardless of sampling: their own message (shown instantly by the client, confirmed by the ack), replies to them and mentions of them, moderator notices, and paid or highlighted messages, which the product sold as guaranteed visibility and which therefore go to everyone, bypassing the sample. The registry of user to edge routes directed messages straight to the right connection; the edge merges the lanes by sequence number.

Reactions: count, don't deliver. At a million reactions per second, each edge keeps a counter per (stream, emote) and every 250 ms sends its counts upstream, then resets. An aggregator merges counts from all edges and publishes the stream's totals (or the rate per emote) every 500 ms through the normal fan-out, where they ride in the same frame as chat. Clients turn the totals into floating hearts and bursts locally. Inbound traffic falls from a million events to a few hundred summaries per second; outbound is one small number set per viewer per half second. The lab shows the same reduction at small scale: 15,000 reactions become 60,000 summary deliveries instead of 45 million individual ones.
